chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ر-د (ṭarada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To drive away, expel, chase; continuity and sequence of a thing following another without interruption.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, co-extensiveness of a descriptive attribute (waṣf) with the legal ruling (ḥukm) — the attribute's presence accompanying the ruling's presence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical expulsion; here used metaphorically (majāz) for logical concomitance and invariable association.
- Root: ع-ك-س (ʿakasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To reverse, invert, turn back; the opposite direction of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Co-exclusiveness — the ruling's absence when the attribute is absent; paired with ṭard to establish causal connection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal reversal; metaphorically, the contrapositive relation in legal reasoning.
- Root: و-ج-د (wajada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To find, perceive, exist; existence (wujūd) as opposed to non-existence (ʿadam).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ontological existence; in causal reasoning, the actualization of a ruling upon the actualization of its attribute.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal finding; here, the technical sense of a ruling's realization contingent upon an attribute's realization.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis Construction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The syntactic linkage of a conditional clause to its apodosis, where the protasis's occurrence entails the apodosis's occurrence, mirroring the causal relation between attribute and ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say — and with God is success:

Know that the co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness (al-ṭard wa al-ʿaks) are mentioned from two aspects: one sound, the other corrupt.

As for the corrupt [aspect], it is: displaying the existence of the ruling upon the existence of an attribute in one locus, and displaying its non-existence upon the non-existence of that attribute in another locus — as the Ḥanafī, for example, says: "Gypsum is measured by volume (makīl), so usury (ribā) applies to it as it applies to wheat." It is then said to him: "Why do you claim that the cause (ʿillah) in wheat is measurement by volume?" He replies: "Because wheat, along with the three [other ribawī] items, being measured and quantified, usury applied to it; while garments and slaves, not being measured and quantified, usury did not apply to them." Thus this attribute was found with the ruling's existence, and absent with its absence.

This and its like are corrupt: because the ruling exists with attributes that are merely coincidental (waṣf ittifāqī) accompanying it, and ceases upon the cessation of coincidental attributes. This arguer was not able to say: "The ruling existed by virtue of its existence, and ceased by virtue of its cessation." Rather, he said: "It existed alongside its existence in one locus, and ceased alongside its cessation in another." And even if this is safe from refutation (naqḍ) in co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness, there is no good in it by way of [true] co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness. It may, however, be relied upon by way of resemblance (shabah), as we shall mention its aspect and modality — God willing. This is one aspect of co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness.

The second aspect: that the arguer is able to claim its existence by virtue of the attribute's existence, and its non-existence by virtue of its non-existence. When this is sound, it is — in our view — a proof that the attribute is a cause (ʿillah).

Rather, we add and say: If his statement "it existed by virtue of its existence" is conceded, that suffices him; he is not required to demonstrate its non-existence by virtue of its non-existence after [establishing] existence. For in [establishing] existence by virtue of its existence, there is [implicitly] the demonstration of non-existence by virtue of its non-existence — since the acceptance of existence was previously non-existent, and its non-existence [now] is by virtue of the non-existence of that by which it existed. This much suffices.

We shall give three examples for this, and arrange the proof upon the establishment of the aspect of the examples:

The first example: We say — the cause in the prohibition of wine (khamr) is intoxication and inebriation (al-shiddah wa al-iskār); for the prohibition exists by virtue of their existence, having been non-existent when it was grape-juice (ʿaṣīr). Nothing new occurred except the intoxicating strength, and prohibition was renewed [with it]. Then it became vinegar (khal), and became lawful — so it ceased by virtue of its cessation. But this addition is unnecessary; for in the renewal of prohibition upon the renewal of intoxicating strength, there is sufficient indication that the intoxicating strength is the cause. We analogize (qiyās) by this linkage all other fermented beverages (anbidhah) to wine.

The second example: The Ḥanafī says regarding the discerning minor (al-ṣabī al-ʿāqil): that contracts are validly concluded by his utterance, because he is discerning (ʿāqil); so contracts are concluded by his utterance, like the adult (bāligh). It is said to him: "What is the proof that discernment (al-ʿaql), in the case of the adult, is the effective basis (manāṭ) for the validity of utterance?" He replies: "It ceased by virtue of its cessation — for when he becomes insane (janna), nothing ceases except discernment; and when he recovers, nothing is renewed except discernment. Thus it existed by virtue of its existence, and ceased by virtue of its cessation."

The third example: We say regarding the slave (al-ʿabd): he is enslaved (raqīq), so the prescribed punishment for fornication (ḥadd al-zinā) is halved in his case, like the female slave (al-amah); and we analogize to the female slave because the textual evidence (naṣṣ) is addressed regarding her — God Most High said: {فإذا أحصن فإن أتين بفاحشة فعليهن نصف ما على المحصنات من العذاب} ("And if they are married, and they commit a lewd act, then upon them is half the punishment of what is upon the chaste women"). It is said: "What is the proof that slavery is the cause?" We say: The halving ceases by virtue of its cessation — for if she were emancipated, her punishment would not be halved.

In these cases: when we demonstrate existence by virtue of the attribute's existence — as in the first case of wine's intoxicating strength and its becoming vinegar — or we demonstrate non-existence by virtue of the attribute's non-existence — as in the cessation of halving upon the cessation of slavery, and the cessation of contractual validity upon the cessation of discernment when insanity supervenes — then the proof is complete that it is a cause, until the opponent demonstrates in disputation, or it becomes evident to the examiner by another examination, that the ruling did not arise upon the arising of this [attribute], but rather arose upon the arising of another meaning (maʿnā) that the new occurrence entails, or a meaning adjacent to the new occurrence; or it arose by it alongside another attribute preceding it in existence; or it arose at its occurrence by another cause prior to it in existence. All these possibilities are open to it. But they do not repel the claim of causal efficacy (taʿlīl) at the inception of examination. Upon whoever claims any of these possibilities rests the burden of proof and the demonstration of suitability (munāsabah).

If it is said: "How do these examples benefit you, when we only concede in them the claim of efficacy by suitability, not by co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness? For the existence of discernment and its absence is suitable to the release of disposition and its restraint; the existence of intoxication is suitable to the prohibition of drinking; and the weak state of the slave is suitable to the mitigation of punishment. Thus reliance is upon suitability. And when suitability is conceded, the claim of causal efficacy is conceded by consensus — so where is the effect of co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness?"

We say: Suitability is operative in these examples. But before the examiner perceives the aspect of suitability, he understands that the ruling only arose upon the arising of an attribute arranged upon it; so that attribute is the effective cause in it, and the necessitator of its occurrence. This is an evident presumption (ẓann) at the inception of examination. If this presumption is reinforced by suitability, it increases in clarity — but it is obtained before suitability. The proof of this is what we have already presented in the pathways of indication (masālik al-īmāʾ): that every ruling arranged upon a cause with the particle of immediate sequence (fāʾ al-taʿqīb), or with the form of condition and consequence (ṣīghat al-sharṭ wa al-jazāʾ), indicates that it is a cause. Like His saying — were this wording to occur: "Whoever has intercourse during the daytime of Ramaḍān, let him expiate." And like the transmitted saying: {من بدل دينه فاقتلوه} ("Whoever changes his religion, kill him"). Its causality is not understood from suitability; rather, it is understood from the linguistic attachment (al-iḍāfah al-lafẓiyyah). The proof is that if He said: "Whoever touches his penis, let him perform ablution," it would be understood as a cause even if there were no suitability. And if He said, for example: "Whoever touches the wall, let him perform ablution," it would be understood that He made touching the wall a cause. Then we add to this and say: When the Messenger of God — peace be upon him — issued a ruling immediately following an incident (wāqiʿah) mentioned to him, the incident is a cause of the ruling — as when the Bedouin said: "I have had intercourse with my wife during the daytime of Ramaḍān," and he said: "Free a slave." It was understood from this that intercourse is the cause of emancipation — and this was not understood by way of suitability, for there is no suitability [apparent]. And if we suppose the narration of a matter with no suitability — as when someone says, for example: "Last night I saw in a dream that I was drinking water from a jug," and the Prophet — peace be upon him — said: "Free a slave" — it would be understood that his vision is a cause, and minds would wonder upon hearing it: by what wisdom was it made a cause with no suitability? The wonder is precisely because of understanding that it was made a cause. This is all what we have already presented. The basis of understanding in it is: the occurrence of the ruling upon the occurrence of the incident, arranged upon it — and this is precisely the co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness that we claim; only the expression differs. For we say: The Bedouin was free of liability (dhimma) from expiation — this is known by law; nothing new occurred from him except intercourse, and the obligation of expiation was renewed — so it existed by virtue of its existence. And implicit in this is that it was non-existent before that by virtue of its non-existence. This is a pathway that makes us know that intercourse is a cause and an effective basis, so that we extend the cause and say: This was reported regarding the Bedouin, so all of creation is annexed to him; or it was reported regarding a free man, so the slave is annexed to him; or it was reported regarding a man, so the woman is annexed to him — on the more apparent opinion; or it was reported regarding intercourse with one's wife, so intercourse with a slave-girl or a foreign woman is annexed to it. The basis of all this is our understanding that the ruling arose upon the arising of intercourse. This is not based on suitability — for this understanding, these very dispositions, and these annexations operate in the case of the dream, for which we have distanced the pursuit in its depiction, to distance the supposition of suitability.

And just as this is known in the incident raised to the Prophet — peace be upon him — it is precisely the same understanding in the occurrence of an attribute upon a locus devoid of the ruling. Grape-juice has no prohibition in drinking it; nothing new occurred except the intoxicating strength, and prohibition was renewed. Thus it is known that it arose upon its arising.

Likewise: the adult — when he becomes insane, his utterance becomes invalid, and nothing ceased except his discernment; for adulthood (bulūgh) did not cease by it. Thus it is known — since it ceased by virtue of its cessation — that it was established by virtue of its existence, and that it is the cause of it. What difference is there between saying to the Messenger — peace be upon him: "The grape-juice has become intoxicating," and he says: "Its drinking is prohibited" — so it is understood that the intoxicating strength is the cause — and between our knowing from law and consensus that whenever grape-juice becomes intoxicating, it is prohibited? For when prohibition is conjoined with intoxicating strength and arises with it, it is known that it necessitates it and is a sign (ʿalāmah) upon it.

Likewise: if the Prophet — peace be upon him — were asked, for example, about a sheep that died: "May it be sold?" and he said: "No" — it would be believed that death is the cause of prohibiting sale — since the permissibility of sale was known before death, and nothing new occurred except death, and the prohibition of sale was renewed — so it is known that it was renewed by its cause. And if it were known by law that when a sheep dies, its sale is prohibited, one would judge that death is the cause — just as in the case of the question and the arrangement of the answer upon it. This is without knowing any suitability of death; rather, no suitability is known for it. The proof of understanding that it is a cause: extending it to camels, cattle, and all other animals, before investigating its suitability and before pausing upon it.

Indeed, if a researcher says: "It is not caused by death per se; rather, it is caused by its exiting from the status of wealth (māliyyah) — for wealth is that from which benefit is derived, and this [dead animal] has no benefit" — this is suitable, intelligible speech; and by it we discern that death is not a cause in itself, but rather a cause for a meaning it entails: namely, the loss of benefits and the nullification of wealth. This parallels our statement that his saying — peace be upon him: {لا يقض القاضي وهو غضبان} ("The judge shall not judge while angry") — indicates causation by anger at first examination; and it is known by second examination that anger is not a cause in itself, but rather a cause for what it entails: weakness of intellect and its bewilderment. We have given examples of this in the attributes to which rulings are attached; this runs in this course.

Then the one who causes by death may nullify this meaning and say: "Its benefit is not lost; for its skin is benefited from after tanning, and its flesh is made fodder for beasts of prey and dogs — and this is an intended purpose. The fodder of animals is wealth for the purpose of feeding animals; likewise the fodder of beasts of prey." Thus this meaning is nullified, and the causation returns to death itself.

Another examiner may say: "Its cause is what death entails: impurity (najāsah)." It would then extend to everything impure, and would not extend to an animal that died without becoming impure — were that conceivable.

This [latter view] concedes — if impurity is suitable to prohibiting sale. If it is not suitable, we return to attachment to death itself.

If it is said: "The inference has returned to 'it arose upon its arising' — and who concedes that? What is conceded is only: it arose with its arising, or at its arising. This attaches to the other aspect that you rejected, in which you made the attribute's existence coincidental."

We say: This is a ruling that arose upon the arising of a matter, so it must be attributed to a new matter (amr ḥādith). And there is no new matter except what we mentioned; so the attribution to it is determined. The proof thus arises from two things: one is the necessity of causation by a new matter; the other is that there is no new matter except what we mentioned.

If it is said: "Who concedes that there is no new matter except what you mentioned? Perhaps another meaning arose alongside this one, hidden from you, and that is the cause; and this apparent [attribute] occurred coincidentally."

We say: We allow that. Upon its claimant is to manifest it. Our allowing it does not cut off the claim of attribution to it — just as if it were suitable, this possibility would not be cut off; rather, the occurrence of a hidden attribute more suitable than what appeared would be possible, making that the cause and this one discarded. But the apparent is the first to presumption (ẓann), so it is the object of attachment until the hidden appears by precise examination. Likewise, the apparent new occurrence is attributed to it at first examination; and this examination is susceptible to corruption by what appears — of another hidden meaning — upon precise examination. But before its appearance, it is the object of attachment. It is a rank in examination by which the foot of the one who causes (al-muʿallil) is established; and the condition of its completion is that nothing else appears, or that what appears besides it is corrupted. As in the suitable [attribute], and as in the linguistic attachment: to anger in prohibiting judgment, and to killing in barring inheritance, and the preceding examples.

If it is said: "The basis in those examples is the linguistic attachment; and in the suggestive attributes (al-awṣāf al-mukhayyilah) it is suitability — that is what establishes the first foot of the one who causes, until he is dislodged from it by a further examination. So what establishes the foot of the one who causes in this station, such that the objector is required to dislodge him from it by a further examination he manifests in his objection?"

We say: The basis in this station is: its occurrence arranged upon it and immediately after its occurrence — as in the Prophet's ruling — peace be upon him — upon the occurrence of an incident: whether the incident is suitable or not suitable, the apparent [presumption] is that the incident in its very form is the cause, until it becomes evident that it is a cause for what it entails of meaning, not in itself and its essence. This presumption is not cut off except by supposing another meaning beyond what appeared. And the possibility of that does not cut off the presumption — for the possibility of another more suitable [attribute] is possible in suitable attributes, and the presumption is not cut off by their possibility and allowance, though it is cut off by their appearance: when they appear.

Do you not see that Abū Ḥanīfah's presumption is apparent in his statement that the cause of the capacity for utterance (ahliyyat al-ʿibārah) is discernment, not adulthood — because adulthood did not cease by insanity; only discernment ceased by it — until it is said to him: "No; rather, something other than discernment ceased: namely, legal obligation (taklīf). For the minor is not legally obligated." By this, the first presumption is cut off, and examination must be redirected to whether legal obligation is more fitting to be the effective basis, or discernment — for legal obligation ceased with the cessation of discernment.

Likewise: if the objector demonstrates that something other than death occurred in the example we gave, we are obliged to examine it, and to weigh death against it, or to abandon causation by death.

If it is said: "Do you allow causation for the prohibition of wine by the specific pungent odor (al-rāʾiḥah al-fāʾiḥah) peculiar to wine, since it arose with the intoxicating strength? For if someone said: 'The prohibition is caused by the specific pungent odor, for it arose, and the ruling arose with it'?"

We say: If it were conceivable that the occurrence of something other than the odor were hidden from an examiner, this would be his first examination — until it becomes evident that what is suitable arose — namely, intoxication — and it is more worthy than it. But this is weak: because a meaning arose alongside it that is more fitting for causation, more apparent to examination, and more prior to knowledge and comprehension. We concede the nullification of this attribution whenever what is more worthy than it appears. But that does not indicate that the first attribution is not on a rank in examination by which the foot is established — just as when the more apparent suitable [attribute] appears, the more hidden suitable one is nullified. By "the more apparent suitable" we mean the stronger that appears second; by "the more hidden" we mean the weaker that appears first.

If it is said: "If the objector demonstrates the occurrence of another meaning that is not suitable, does it nullify the first examination?"

We say: If the first is not suitable, they are equal; neither is more worthy than the other. Upon the one who causes is weighing and disengagement (al-tarjīḥ wa al-infiṣāl). If the second is suitable, it becomes — by virtue of its suitability alone — preferred over the first apparent [attribute] that is not suitable. If the first is suitable, they are equal; upon the one who causes is weighing. If it is stronger than the first, it is weighed over it by its strength. Thus the non-suitable equals the non-suitable in this station — just as the suitable equals the suitable.

And in this station, what we are discussing — existence by the occurrence of the attribute — departs from the linguistic attachment. For if someone said: "Anger is not a cause in itself; rather, it is for a meaning it entails or that is adjacent to it; and that meaning is also not suitable — like anger, for example" — it is discarded, and we attach to the explicitly uttered attribute (al-waṣf al-manṭūq bihi): because its utterance is a proof (ḥujjah).

As for here: there is no utterance; the basis is only the occurrence of the ruling upon its occurrence. And two attributes have occurred; so attribution to one of them is arbitrary. Indeed, it is as if attributed to one: for it is the apparent only. When the opponent alerts to the second attribute, the first presumption is nullified, and weighing is needed. There is no weighing by occurrence, and no weighing by the fact that the first is what appeared first — for precedence and posteriority in appearance vary by persons and aspects of investigation. That does not revert to the strength of the meaning. So what appears second — after its appearance — equals what appeared first.

Thus the form of the questioner's [address] to the Lawgiver — in this matter — attaches to the linguistic attachment, not to the existential attachment that we are discussing. For the arrangement of the ruling upon the questioner's uttered words is like its arrangement upon his own speech. There is no difference — between the questioner saying: "The grape-juice has become intoxicating," and the Lawgiver saying: "It is prohibited," and his saying: "When the grape-juice becomes intoxicating, it is prohibited" — in that the apparent [presumption] is that the intoxicating strength is the cause, even if it is not suitable. And no other meaning that is neither adjacent to it nor suitable to it resists it — because it was not uttered.

If it is said: "It is possible that the cause is the new attribute alongside another attribute that is continuous in this very locus; and the ruling attached to two attributes: it exists upon the supervention of one after the precedence of the first, and ceases upon its cessation; then it does not follow that single attribute without the conjunction of the other attribute to it. Its example: if the Lawgiver explicitly stated that the cause is the intoxicating strength of grape-juice, the ruling would exist upon the existence of the strength and cease upon its non-existence; yet the strength would not be followed in other than grape-juice — because being grape-juice is an essential attribute (waṣf dhātī) continuous in it, and the other is an accident that supervenes and departs. The ruling is suspended upon the accidental attribute. When one of the two attributes is continuous and the other accidental — supervening and departing — the ruling revolves with the accidental and departs with its departure; for it is attached to the conjunction of the two attributes: in its occurrence is the conjunction, and in its departure is the departure of the conjunction."

We say: This is conceded; we do not deny it. But in allowing it, there is nothing that cuts off the presumption from following the new attribute. For the suitable meaning — likewise — does not prevent another attribute from being with it that increases suitability, with the ruling arranged upon the conjunction of the two attributes. But when one suitable [attribute] appears, the demand is cut off from it; upon the opponent is to alert to the additional one conjoined to it, until he disengages from it.

Indeed, if he is a mujtahid, he ought to investigate. If the manifestation of a second attribute is difficult, he restricts himself to the first. If he is a disputant (muʿallil), he mentions what appeared, and his foot is established in the first examination. Upon the opponent is to alert him to the second attribute, until he speaks upon it.

Likewise, the mujtahid in our question: he investigates and reflects; perhaps he stumbles upon another attribute. If he does not stumble, he relies upon the new attribute. If he is a disputant, that new attribute suffices him. Upon the objector is to say: "What secures you from the possibility that such-and-such attribute is conjoined to your attribute?" When he mentions this much, disengagement is incumbent upon him. If he does not mention it, and says: "Perhaps another attribute hidden from you is latent, conjoined to your attribute — what secures you from it?" — he is not obliged to answer this, as in the case of the suitable [attribute].

If it is said: "The ruling appears upon the occurrence of the condition (sharṭ) when the cause is prior, just as it appears upon the occurrence of the cause. Thus whoever purchases his relative: the relative is emancipated upon him. Emancipation occurred upon the occurrence of purchase and ownership together; yet ownership is not the cause of emancipation — the cause is kinship. But kinship is a continuous essential attribute: it neither supervenes nor departs; while ownership supervenes and departs. So the ruling appeared upon the appearance of the condition — which is the locus of the cause, not the cause itself."

We say: This is of the kind of the previous question. The mujtahid must investigate the latent attributes other than the new attribute. If an attribute appears that equals the new one, he makes the cause composite of the two attributes. If a suitable attribute appears, he makes it the cause and makes the new one a condition — as in the purchase of the relative. If nothing appears, he makes the new attribute the effective basis (manāṭ) of the ruling and its sign (ʿalam), and attributes the ruling to it.

In all cases, it is not permissible to nullify the new attribute by which the ruling appeared: either it is considered a cause, or a condition of a cause, or a cause [itself]. The first examination requires referring to it and supposing its independence in producing the ruling. If this examination remains sound — in the second and third ranks — from examination of what diminishes it, it stands; otherwise, judgment is given by what appeared second.

The purpose is that the causes are cut off from the demand [for proof], and no demand is directed upon them — as long as the objector does not alert to another attribute conjoined to it: either supposing it an attribute or an independent cause; or supposing that other attribute an independent principle (aṣl), with the new one coincidental and adjacent.

As long as he does not alert to any of that, his demand is not directed. This is the purpose. For if it remains sound in the second rank of examination, and nothing else appears — it is permissible for the mujtahid [to rely upon it].

chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ص-ص (kha-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of exclusivity, singling out, or particularization — the act of distinguishing one thing from another by a specific attribute or ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, *takhṣīṣ* denotes the restriction of a general ruling (ʿāmm) to a specific subject (maḥall), often due to a distinguishing cause (ʿillah) or textual indicator.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is physical or conceptual isolation; metaphorical (majāz) sense applies to legal specification where the ruling is tied to a particular locus without altering the general principle.
- Root: س-أ-ل (sa-ʾ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To ask, inquire, or demand — here, a formal dialectical question (suʾāl) posed as an objection in jurisprudential debate.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām and uṣūl al-fiqh, a *suʾāl* is a structured interrogative seeking clarification or challenging a claim, often requiring a *jawāb* (answer) that resolves the apparent inconsistency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is verbal inquiry; metaphorical sense is the intellectual demand for justification, as in "the question calls for" (yadʿū ilā) — a causal prompting.
- Root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Judgment, ruling, or governance — the authoritative determination of a legal or theological matter.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): *Ḥukm* is the divine or juristic decision that attaches to an act or object, here specifically the legal ruling (ḥukm sharʿī) that is subject to specification.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is arbitration; metaphorical sense is the legal verdict that "descends" upon a locus (maḥall), implying a relational attachment.
- Root: م-ح-ل (ma-ḥ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Place, locus, or site — the physical or conceptual location where something resides.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, *maḥall* is the subject or substrate upon which a ruling operates, distinct from the cause (ʿillah) that generates it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is spatial; metaphorical sense is the "seat" of a ruling, i.e., the specific case or object to which the law applies.
- Sībawayh Rule: *Al-Muḍāf wa al-Muḍāf Ilayh* (Construct State) — The phrase "سؤال يدعو إلى تخصيص الحكم بالمحل" employs a nominal sentence where the subject (sūʾāl) is qualified by a verbal clause (yadʿū ilā), indicating a causal relationship; the preposition "bi-" in "bi-l-maḥall" marks the instrument or attachment, requiring precise parsing to avoid ambiguity between the ruling's locus and its cause.
chapters.translation:
I say: This is a question that prompts the specification of the ruling to its locus, and its answer follows.

Know that the questioner may object: "Why is the ruling confined to this particular locus (maḥall), rather than extending to another, given that the cause (ʿillah) appears common?" The answer is that the specification (takhṣīṣ) is not arbitrary but is grounded in the distinguishing attribute (al-mukhayyil) that the Lawgiver has established as the indicator of the ruling. For the ruling does not attach to the locus merely by virtue of its existence, but by virtue of the meaning (maʿnā) that resides in it, which is the true cause. Thus, when the question calls for specification, it seeks to uncover that meaning, and the answer lies in demonstrating that the specified locus alone possesses the attribute that renders it fit for the ruling, while other loci lack it. This is the method of the scholars of uṣūl, who distinguish between the locus as a mere container and the locus as a bearer of the effective cause. Therefore, the specification is not a defect in the ruling but a precision in its application, and the answer to the question is the clarification of the cause's exclusivity to that locus, either by textual indication (dalīl naqlī) or by rational inference (dalīl ʿaqlī), as the principles of legal causality (al-ʿillah al-sharʿiyyah) demand.

chapters.title_en: The Attainment of Legal Causality Through the Description Originating with the Ruling
chapters.arabic_text:
أن يجعل الوصف الحادث علما على الحكم متبعا، كما في ترتيب الجواب من
الشارع على الواقعة، وكما في الترتيب اللفظي بفاء التعقيب، فإن الإضافة إلى
الشرط [لفظا] جائز، كما يجوز إلى العلة، ولكن الأصل: أن المضاف إليه هو
الموجب، إلى أن يظهر وصف هو أولى بالإيجاب منه، فكذلك ما نحن فيه.
فإن قيل: إذا جوزتم أن يعلل بالوصف الحادث وإن كان لا يناسب، فم ينكر
العلل على المعترض إذا قال له: سلمت لك أنه سبب، ولكنه  سبب في هذا المحلل
على الخصوص، كقوله: سلمت [لك] أن الشدة سبب، ولكن السبب شدة عصير العنب،
[فبم تنكر عليه]: وغايتك أن تقول: هذا تخصيص بوصف أو بمحل لا مدخل له ولا
تأثير له في إيجاب الحكم؛ على معنى أنه لا يناسب، فأصل الوصف - أيضا - غير
[45 - أ] مناسب، وإضافة الحكم إليه على مذاق التحكمات التي لا تعقل، ولا
فرق بينه وبين التخصيص بهذا المحل. وفيه ما يمنع الإنتفاع بجنس هذا
التعليل، ويقصر الحكم على محل النص والإجماع؟.
وهذا هو السؤال الأعظم على هذه القاعدة، [و] في دفعة تمهيد هذا الأصل
وتقريره.
قلنا: نتكلم على هذا السؤال، من وجهين:
أحدهما: هو أن يقال: يجب على المعلل أن يبين أن هذا الحكم ليس PageV01P284 # مخصوصا بالمحل ومقتصرا على الذات [التي فيها] الإجماع؛ وإذا بطل ذلك:
وجبت الإضافة إلى صفة متعدية. فبطل به الاختصاص. وهذا كقولنا: صوم مفروض،
فيفتقر إلى التبييت كالقضاء. فيقول الخصم: لا مناسبة لكونه مفروضا؛ أن علة
وجوب التبييت في القضاء كونه مفروضا، وهو لا يناسب؟ [لا]، بل العلة فيه
كونه قضاء، حتى يقتصر عليه. فيقال: وبالإجماع التبييت ليس مخصوصا بوصف كونه
قضاء، فإن النذر والكفاءة وسائر الصيام يشترط فيه التبييت؛ فبطل التخصيص
بالمحل والذات، ووجب التعليل بوصف يتعدى.
وكذلك إذا قلنا: أن المستعير يضمن، لأنه أثبت يده على مال غيره لغرض
نفسه، من غير استحقاق؛ فيضمن كالمستام. فقيل لنا: هذا الوصف PageV01P285 # ليس علة في المستام؛ لأنه لا يناسب، فينبغي أن يقال: أنه غير معقول، ليس
علة في السنسام؛ لأنه لا يناسب، فينبغي أن يقال: أنه غير معقول، أو هو
مخصوص بمحله وصورته، وهو: يد السوم، فيقال: وبالإجماع ضمان الأيدي غير
مقصود على يد السو؛ إذ هو جار في يد الشراء، ويد المستعير من الغاصب، ويد
المودع إذا جحد، ويد الغاصب وغيره، فاجتمع أمران، أحدهما: وجوب التعليل؛
[والآخر] الإضافة إلى الوصف الحادث: لأن الحكم حدث بحدوث وصف، وهذا مما يجب
تعليله؛ فقد كان الرجل بريء الذمة، تضمن بالأخذ؛ فأضيف إلى  الأخذ، ووجب سير
صفاته؛ وامتنع تخصيصه بمحله بالإجماع. لذلك فلم يبطل تعليلنا به: لأن ذلك
متفوض بالإجماع؛ وكل وصف انتقض بالإجماع فقد بان بالإجماع أنه ليس مناطا
للحكم؛ حتى [لو] عللنا الضمان في يد السوم: بأنه إثبات يد على مال الغير؛
وتركنا خصوص جهة السوم - لبطل بيد الوديعة؛ فلابد أن نزيد، فتقول: أثبت
إليه لغرض نفسه؛ احترازا عن الوديعة. وهو أيضا منقوض بيد الإجارة، فلابد
وأن نزيد قولنا: من غير استحقاق؛ فاستقام التعليل بهذا القدر - وإن كان لا
يناسب -: من حيث أن الحكم [حدث] مع حدوث سبب فعرف PageV01P286 # ارتباطه [به]. فنظرنا في تنقيح المناط وتهذيبه وتحديده، فاستقام ما
ذكرناه بعد وجوب التعدية من محل الإجماع - وهو [جهة] السوم - بطريق
المناقضة التي ذكرناها.
نعم: لو اقتبس الخصم من يد السوم وصفا آخر: يطر له أيضا، ولا يتنقض، ولا
يتعدى إلى العارية - كان مقاوما معارضا لكلامنا، وعلينا الترجيح.
وهذا كقوله: ان المستام إنما ضمن: لأنه أخذ بجهة الشراء، والشراء جهة
ضمان: والمأخوذ على جهة الشيء: كالمأخوذ على حقيقته؛ وتعدى هذا إلى يد
الرهن، وتقطع عنه يد العارية. فهذا يقاوم كلامنا إلى أن نرجع جانبا بطريقه.
وعلى المجتهد البحث عن هذه المعارضات وتعيين واحد منها بالترجيح؛ وليس على
المعلل ذلك، بل كفاه أن يذكر وصفا يدعي ظهوره [له] إلى أن يقابل بغيره:
فيتكلم عليه.
ولا ينبغي أن يتخيل الناظر [أن النظر] في هذا المثال، استقام: لكون
الأوصاف فيها مناسبة؛ إذ لا مناسبة لها؛ وإن ظن ظان أن فيها مناسبة، فهذا
المنهاج جار قبل العثور على وجه المناسبة؛ فليقدر عدم المناسبة PageV01P287 # التي يتخيلها: فإن غرضنا المثال.
وكذلك: قاس الشافعي - رضى الله عنه - تعذر الثمن بإفلاس المشتري، على
تعذر العبد المبيع بالإباق؛ وهذا حكم واجب التعليل والإضافة: فإن الخيار
حدث بحدوث الإباق، فدل أنه السبب بعينه أو بما يتضمنه، فلم يختص بإباق
العيد في البيع - وهو أخص [45 - ب] الصفات - إذ هو جار في إباق الجارية،
وجار في نفار الدابة وطيران الطير؛ بل هو جار  في غضب المنقولات؛ فوجبت
التعدية، فقيل: الشامل لجميع هذه الصور: تعذر العوض. فكان الإباق علة بهذا
الاعتبار؛ وقد تعذر الثمن بالإفلاس.
ثم هذا القدر يبطل بتعذر إستيفاء الصداق: فإنه لا يثبت الخيار في النكاح؛
وتعذر استيفاء البضع بالإباق لا يوجب الفسخ. فوجب أن نزيد، PageV01P288 # فنقول: تعذر عوض في عقد بيع، فيبطل الخصوص بالإجماع، ويجب التعليل للحدوث
بحدوث الوصف، فيه يدفع السؤال.
ثم الخصم أن يقيد هذا الوصف بقيد آخر: يتعدى محل النص، ولكن لا يتعدى إلى
محل النزاع، وهو أن يقول: تعذر في عين، فلا يتعدى إلى الثمن وهو دين؛
وعلينا أن نتكلم عليه بالإبطال أو الترجيح، فنقول: ليس مخصوصا بالعين؛ إذ
يتعدى إلى المسلم فيه: إذا انقطع جنسه، وهو دين؛ فيقول: تعذر في عوض مقصود
هو محل العقد، والثمن ليس محلا للعقد؛ فينكر ذلك، فنقول: بل هو محل العقد؛
فالثمن والمثمن عوضان يتعادلان عندنا، فنذهب في الاستدلال بالشواهد على
كونه محل العقد، ويذهب في معارضته.
وقد يغير العبارة، ويقول: العلة تعذر في مقصود قبل القبض تعين فيه القبض؛
ويخرج عليه المسلم فيه؛ وتنعكس العلة في الثمن: فإنه لا يتعين فيه القبض؛
إذ يجوز الاعتياض عنه. فنتكلم عليه بالمنع أو بالإبطال أو بالترجيح.
هكذا تقوم مراتب النظر بين المتناظرين في الأحكام الحادثة بحدوث الأوصاف؛
وهي التي وجب إضافتها إلى الحادث، ورجع النظر إلى
PageV01P289
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Repetition and succession; a secondary cause or attribute that recurs with its effect; the "cause" (ʿillah) as that which is repeated with the ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The theological-legal sense: the effective attribute (waṣf muʾaththir) that necessitates a ruling (ḥukm) by divine law, not by nature.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a recurring illness or defect; metaphorical (majāz): the legal cause as a "marker" (amārah) for the ruling, not a true efficient cause.
- Root: خ-ص-ص (kh-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To single out, to distinguish; particularization (takhṣīṣ) of a ruling to a specific case or attribute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Restriction of a universal divine command to a limited subject-matter, as opposed to taʿmīm (generalization).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a private portion; metaphorical: confining a legal ratio to its textual locus (maḥall al-naṣṣ).
- Root: ن-ق-ض (n-q-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To break, to undo; in legal theory: refutation by counter-example (naqḍ) where the alleged cause exists but the ruling does not.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The invalidation of a claimed causal link by showing its inconsistency across cases.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: unraveling a woven fabric; metaphorical: dismantling an opponent's argument by exposing its internal contradiction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-ḥukm ʿalā al-waṣf (Conditional attachment of the ruling to the attribute) — The ruling is syntactically and logically annexed to the originating description, as in conditional clauses with faʿ al-taʿqīb (the particle fa indicating immediate succession), where the protasis marks the cause of the apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The originating description may be made a sign (ʿalam) for the ruling, following it, just as the Lawgiver's response is ordered upon the occurrence, and just as in verbal ordering with the particle of immediate succession (fāʾ al-taʿqīb). For annexing [the ruling] to the condition is permissible in wording, just as it is permissible to annex it to the cause. But the principle is: that to which annexation is made is the obligating factor (mūjib), until an attribute appears that is more deserving of obligating than it. So likewise is our case here.

If it is said: "When you permit causation by an originating description even though it is not suitable (munāsib), then what do you say against the objector's causes when he says to you: 'I grant you that it is a cause, but it is a cause in this particular locus (maḥall) specifically' — as when he says: 'I grant you that intensity (shiddah) is a cause, but the cause is the intensity of grape-juice specifically'? For your utmost is to say: 'This is a particularization by an attribute or by a locus that has no entry and no effect in obligating the ruling' — meaning that it is not suitable. But the original attribute itself is also not suitable, and annexing the ruling to it is in the manner of arbitrary determinations (taḥakkumāt) that are not intelligible. There is no difference between it and particularization by this locus. And in this there is what prevents benefit from this entire genus of causation, and confines the ruling to the locus of the text and consensus (ijmāʿ)?"

This is the greatest question against this principle, and in repelling it lies the establishment of this foundation and its consolidation.

We say: We shall address this question from two angles:

The first: It is to be said: The one who asserts causation (al-muʿallil) must demonstrate that this ruling is not particular to the locus nor confined to the very entity [concerning which] there is consensus. When that is invalidated, annexation to a transgressive attribute (ṣifah mutaʿaddiyah) becomes obligatory, and thereby the particularization is nullified. This is like our saying: "A prescribed fast (ṣawm mafrūḍ) requires intention by night (tabyīt), like the make-up fast (qaḍāʾ)." The opponent then says: "There is no suitability in its being prescribed; that the cause of the obligation of tabyīt in the make-up fast is its being prescribed — but that is not suitable. Rather, the cause therein is its being a make-up (qaḍāʾ), so that it is confined to it." Then it is said: "By consensus, tabyīt is not particular to the attribute of being a make-up, for the vowed fast (nadhr), the expiatory fast (kaffārah), and all other fasts require tabyīt. Thus particularization by locus and entity is nullified, and causation by a transgressive attribute becomes obligatory."

Likewise, when we say: "The borrower (mustaʿīr) is liable (yaḍman) because he placed his hand upon another's property for his own purpose, without entitlement; so he is liable like the one who inspects for purchase (mustām)." Then it is said to us: "This attribute is not a cause in the mustām, because it is not suitable; so it should be said that it is unintelligible (ghayr maʿqūl), or it is particular to its locus and form, namely, the hand of inspection (yad al-sawm)." Then it is said: "By consensus, liability of hands (ḍamān al-aydī) is not confined to the hand of inspection, for it runs in the hand of purchase, the hand of the borrower from the usurper (ghāṣib), the hand of the depositary (wadīʿ) when he denies [the deposit], the hand of the usurper, and others." Thus two matters converge: one is the obligation of causation; the other is annexation to the originating description — because the ruling originated with the origination of a description, and this is something whose causation is obligatory. For the man was free of liability (barīʾ al-dhimmah), then he became liable by taking; so it was annexed to the taking, and the traversal of its attributes became obligatory, and its particularization to its locus was prevented by consensus. Therefore our causation by it was not nullified, because that is delegated to consensus. And every attribute that is refuted (intuqiḍa) by consensus has been shown by consensus not to be the locus of the ruling (manāṭ). Thus, had we caused liability in the hand of inspection by "placing a hand upon another's property" and omitted the specific aspect of inspection, it would have been refuted by the hand of deposit (yad al-wadīʿah). So we must add, saying: "He placed it for his own purpose" — as a precaution against the deposit. But this too is refuted by the hand of hire (yad al-ijārah). So we must further add our saying: "Without entitlement." Thus the causation becomes sound with this measure — even though it is not suitable — by virtue of the fact that the ruling originated with the origination of the cause, so its connection (irtibāṭ) was known. Then we examined the refinement of the locus (tanqīḥ al-manāṭ), its purification (tahdhīb), and its delimitation (taḥdīd), and what we mentioned became sound after the obligation of traversal from the locus of consensus — namely, the aspect of inspection — by way of the contradiction (munāqaḍah) we mentioned.

Indeed, if the opponent were to derive from the hand of inspection another attribute that also applies to it, is not refuted, and does not traverse to the loan (ʿāriyah) — then he would be a rival opposing our statement, and upon us is the weighing (tarjīḥ).

This is like his saying: "The mustām is only liable because he took by way of purchase, and purchase is a ground of liability; and what is taken upon the ground of a thing is like what is taken upon its reality." This traverses to the hand of pledge (rahn) and is cut off from the hand of loan. So this rivals our statement until we return to one side by its method. And upon the mujtahid is the search for these rival considerations and the designation of one of them by weighing. It is not upon the one asserting causation to do that; rather, it suffices him to mention an attribute whose preponderance he claims until it is countered by another, whereupon he addresses it.

And the observer should not imagine that the examination in this example was sound because the attributes therein are suitable; for they have no suitability. Even if one supposes that there is suitability in them, this methodology runs before arriving at the face of suitability. So let him suppose the absence of the suitability he imagines, for our purpose is the example.

Likewise, al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — analogized the failure of the price (taʿadhdhur al-thaman) due to the buyer's bankruptcy (iflās) to the failure of the sold slave due to flight (ibāq). This is a ruling whose causation and annexation are obligatory: for the option (khiyār) originated with the origination of the flight, so it indicated that it is the very cause or what it entails. It was not particular to the flight of the slave in sale — which is the most specific of attributes — for it runs in the flight of the slave-girl, runs in the shying of the beast and the flying of the bird; rather, it runs in the loss of movables. So traversal became obligatory, and it was said: "What encompasses all these forms is the failure of the counter-value (taʿadhdhur al-ʿiwaḍ)." Thus flight was a cause by this consideration, and the price failed by bankruptcy.

Then this measure is nullified by the failure of receiving the dowry (ṣadāq): for it does not establish the option in marriage (nikāḥ); and the failure of receiving the sexual enjoyment (baḍʿ) by flight does not necessitate annulment (faskh). So we must add, saying: "Failure of a counter-value in a contract of sale." Thus particularity is nullified by consensus, and causation becomes obligatory for the origination by the origination of the attribute, and thereby the question is repelled.

Then the opponent may restrict this attribute with another restriction that traverses the locus of the text but does not traverse to the locus of dispute — namely, his saying: "Failure in a specific thing (ʿayn)," so it does not traverse to the price, which is a debt (dayn). And upon us is to address it by nullification (ibṭāl) or weighing (tarjīḥ). So we say: "It is not particular to the specific thing, for it traverses to the salam commodity (muslam fīh) when its species is cut off, and it is a debt." Then he says: "Failure in an intended counter-value that is the locus of the contract, and the price is not a locus of the contract." This is denied, and we say: "Rather, it is a locus of the contract; for the price and the priced are two counter-values that are equivalent in our view." So we proceed in adducing evidences (shawāhid) for its being a locus of the contract, and he proceeds in countering it.

And he may change the expression and say: "The cause is failure in an intended thing before receipt (qabḍ) in which receipt is determined (taʿayyana)." The salam commodity comes out under this. And the cause is reversed in the price: for receipt is not determined therein, since substitution for it is permissible. So we address it by prevention (manʿ), nullification (ibṭāl), or weighing (tarjīḥ).

Thus the ranks of examination (marātib al-naẓar) stand between the two disputants concerning rulings that originate with the origination of attributes — these being the rulings to which annexation to the originating [description] is obligatory, and the examination returns to the refinement of the locus and its determination, as we have set forth.

chapters.title_en: On Requiring a Specific Indicator That the Original Ruling Is Effectuated by a Cause, and al-Ghazālī’s Directing of That
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| CHECK إشتراط دليل خاص على أن الأصل معلول بعلة، وتوجيه الغزالي لذلك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Repetition of an ailment or recurrent condition; secondary occurrence; that which necessitates a subsequent state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, ʿillah denotes the effective cause that renders a ruling (ḥukm) attached to an act, distinct from mere occasion (sabab) or sign (amārah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is medical recurrence; metaphorical (majāz) transfer to legal causality is well-established, yet requires explicit textual or rational indication (dalīl) to affirm its operative status.
- Root: ش-ر-ط (sh-r-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Marking, conditioning, or stipulating a prerequisite; that without which something is not valid.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, sharṭ is a condition whose absence entails non-existence of the conditioned, but whose presence does not necessitate it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a sign or notch; metaphorical: a stipulated prerequisite in argumentation.
- Root: أ-ص-ل (a-ṣ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Base, foundation, root; the original case from which analogy (qiyās) proceeds.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The aṣl is the established ruling (ḥukm) in the primary text (naṣṣ) or consensus (ijmāʿ), whose cause is sought for extension.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: root of a tree; metaphorical: the foundational legal case.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-sharṭ ʿalā al-ism al-mawṣūf (Conditional attachment to a qualified noun) — The phrase "دليل خاص" (specific indicator) is a qualified noun (mawṣūf) whose qualification restricts the scope of the required proof, indicating that not any indicator suffices, but only one that specifically demonstrates the causal efficacy of the original ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the verification of legal analogy (qiyās) requires that the original case (al-aṣl) be effectuated by a cause (ʿillah) — that is, that its ruling be attached to it by virtue of a specific attribute (waṣf) that is the effective motive (bāʿith) for the legislation. And this causal efficacy is not to be affirmed merely by the existence of the ruling, nor by the mere suitability (munāsabah) of an attribute, nor by its prevalence (ṭard) or its co-extensiveness (ʿaks). Rather, it is required that there be a specific indicator (dalīl khāṣṣ) — whether from the text (naṣṣ), from consensus (ijmāʿ), or from a rational consideration (iʿtibār) that the Lawgiver (al-Shāriʿ) has made that attribute the cause, such that the ruling is established upon it and is absent when it is absent, in the manner that the cause necessitates its effect.

And al-Ghazālī — may God have mercy on him — directs this requirement by explaining that the mere presence of a ruling in the original case does not, by itself, prove that it is caused, for the ruling might be attached to the original case by way of a specific text (naṣṣ) without any cause, or by way of a divine favor (faḍl) or a pure act of will (mašīʾah) that is not reducible to an attribute. Thus, the one who seeks to extend the ruling to a branch case (al-farʿ) must first establish, through a specific indicator, that the original ruling is indeed caused, and that the attribute he identifies is the very cause intended by the Lawgiver. For if this is not established, the analogy is void, because the extension (taʿdiyah) presupposes the causal link (al-ʿillah) in the original, and the causal link is not to be assumed without proof.

And this is the purport of the section, and God knows best.

chapters.title_en: The Specification of Attributes in Legal Causality and the Role of Occasionality (Munāsabah)
chapters.arabic_text:
تعيين وصف من الحادث، أو إلى تنقيح جملته: بإلغاء بعض، وإبقاء بعض. فكل
ذلك جار دون المناسبة، وقبل العثور على المناسبة؛ ومعظم الأحكام القياسية
من هذا القبيل: فإنها أحكام حدثت بحدوث أسباب موجبة وقع النظر: في تعيين
الأوصاف من الموجبات الحادثة، أو في تنقيحها.
وقد رجع حاصل هذا الجواب، إلى أن السؤال الدعاي إلى تخصيص الحكم بالمحل
لازم، ولكن تبين سقوطه بالإجماع، وهو كمعارضة أخرى تقاوم الوصف المذكور: في
أنه [لا] يناسب؛ فإنه يندفع بالنقض: بالإجماع، أو بمسلك من الترجيح، وذلك
جار بين الوصف المتعدي  وبين الوصف القاصر.
وقد قال قائلون: المتعدي أولى من القاصر في العلل، والمتعدي إلى فروع
أولى من المتعدي إلى فرع واحد؛ يحصل الترجيح بمجرد التعدية.
والجواب الثاني - وهو المختار: أنه إذا اتفق شيء مما ذكرناه في الجواب
الأول: من دلالة الإجماع على بطلان التخصيص؛ فهو ظاهر جلي لا شك فيه، ولكن
ليس ذلك مشروطا.
وقد شرطه فريق؛ إذ قد نقل عن بشر المريسي وجماعة، أنهم قالوا: لا يجوز
القياس على أصل، بمجرد قيام الدليل على أصل تجويز PageV01P290 # القياس، بل لابد وأن يدل دليل خاص على أن الأصل - الذي عليه القياس -
معمول بعلة، فأنا -[مع] ورود الدليل على أصل القياس - نجوز أن يكون من
جملتها أصل لا يعلل، بل يخصص بمورده، فلابد من دليل على كون الأصل معللا.
ولست أعرف لهذا المذهب وجها إلا ما ذكرته، فإن الوصف المخصص إذا عادل
الوصف المتعدي: في الانفكاك عن المناسبة، تقاوما. فلابد من دليل على
التعدية.
فإن خصص صاحب هذا المذهب مذهبه بهذا الجنس: من التعليل الخالي عن
المناسبة؛ فله وجه. ووجهه بين كما ذكرناه.
وإن طرده فيما ظهرت فيه المعاني المناسبة، وقال: يجوز أن يلحظ الشرع
المناسب في محل مخصوص؛ فلابد من دليل التعدية؛ أو قال: يجوز أن يقدر وقوع
هذا المناسب وفاقيا - فهو في هذا الطرف أضعف، واستمداده من القول بإنكار
أصل القياس. وإليه أشار نفاة القياس: في وجوب الاقتصار.
[وعلى الجملة: هذا] المذهب غير سديد في جميع الصور؛ فلا تشترط دلالة
الإجماع على التعدية؛ ولو اتفقت: فهو الأعلى PageV01P291 # والأوضح. ولكنا نقول: إذا حدث وصف، وحدث عقبه حكم [46 - أ] دل حدوثه عقيب
حدوثه، على أن الوصف الحادث: مناطه؛ وأن الحكم يتبع الوصف دون المحل. ثم إن
كان الوصف مناسبا: ظهر تسميته علة، وإن لم يكن مناسبا: فالظاهر أن الحكم
مضاف إليه؛ ويحتمل أن لا يسميه علة من يفهم من العلة المناسبة؛ ويحتمل أن
يسميه علة من يفهم من العلة العلامة؛ ويحتمل أن يجعل اسم العلة له مجازا
والمناسب حقيقة؛ فإن المناسب  عرف وجه تأثيره في الحكم، وهذا لم يعرف وجه
تأثيره، ولكنا نظن أنه متضمن للمعنى المناسب المصلحي الذي لم نطلع عليه،
فهذا الوصف أمارة تلك المصلحة التي غابت عنا وعلامتها، ونظن أنه لا تنفك
عنه في غالب الأحوال، وتنزل منزلة القالب والظرف، فتسميته علة: بطريق تضمنه
للعلة - على طريق المجاز - ليس بعيدا.
وهذا الاختلاف يرجع إلى التسمية، وقد صرح الأصوليون بهذا الاختلاف؛ ولا
خير فيه، فإن العلامات المنصوبة من جهة الشرع متبعة: سواء ناسبت ما هي
علامة عليه، أو لم تناسب؛ فلا ينبغي أن تسوى القواعد على [الألفاظ؛ بل
ينبغي أن تسوى الألفاظ] على المعاني.
PageV01P292
فإذا رجع حاصل النظر إلى أن العلم على الحكم الحادث هو الوصف الحادث:
الذي ظهر في أول النظر حدوثه؛ وأن الحكم يتبع الوصف دون المحل، فالإضافة
إلى المحل ساقطة: عند ظهور العلامة، كما أنها ساقطة عند ظهور المناسبة.
فإن قال قائل: فهذه حكاية المذهب، فماذا دليلكم عليه؟
قلنا: اشتمل المذهب على دعويين. ففي ماذا النزاع؟ - إحداهما: أن الوصف
الظاهر حدوثه علامة؛ والأخرى: أن الحكم يتبع العلامة، دون المحل الذي
العلامة ظهرت فيه.
فإن نوزعنا في قولنا: إن الوصف الحادث علامة، فدليله ما سبق: من أن حدوثه
بحدوثه [دل عليه] كما في الإضافة اللفظية، وكما في حكم الرسول - عليه
السلام - عند وقوع واقعة جديدة، بحكم جديد.
والدليل عليه: أنه لو علم مثلا أن لا حادث إلا الوصف الذي ذكرناه، لوجبت
الإضافة إليه. فإن أصل التعليل والإضافة واجب قطعا بحدوثه بعد أن لم يكن؛
فافتقر إلى محدث: يتميز به عما قبل الأحداث، فلو لم يعلل، لبطل قولنا: أن
الإضافة واجبة. وهو معقول، ولو لم يعلل بهذا الحادث، لبطل قولنا: أن لا
حادث سواه. هذا: إذ علم - بسير قطعي - أن لا حادث سواه.
PageV01P293
فإن لم يعلم، وكان ذلك مظنونا - كفى ذلك المجتهد؛ ويكتفي من المعلل بأن
يعين وصفا يزعم: أنه لم يظهر له سواه؛ [إلى أن ينبه على وصف آخر ظهر سواه]:
فيلزمه أن يتكلم عليه.
ولا تتوجه  عليه المطالبة بأن يقال له: ولم قلت: أن لا حادث سوى ما ذكرت،
ولعله حدث وصف غاب عنك؛ لأنه لو فتح هذا الباب في الجدال: لا تحسم طريق
النظر، ولتوجه ذلك على كل من بيدي المناسب، ولقيل له: أتسلم بطلان علتك
المناسبة لو ظهرت علة أخرى أظهر [مناسبة] مما تدعيه؟ على ما تقرر: من
استحالة تعليل الحكم بعلتين عرفنا بطريق المناسبة؛ فإذا قال: نعم، فيقال:
وما الذي يؤمنك من وجود مناسب أظهر مما تدعيه وأقوى، ولم تطلع عليه؟ فهذا
السؤال مدفوع في الجدال.
وقد قال القاضي أبو بكر: يجب السير على العلل، وهو: أن ينصب علته، ويبين
انتفاء ما عداها. وطرد هذا في المناسب أيضا.
وهو بعيد في حق المجادل، متجه في [حق] المجتهد؛ إذ على المجتهد تمام
النظر: لتحل له الفتوى؛ وليس على المعلل إلا ارتقاء مرتبة PageV01P294 # من مراتب النظر، إلى أن يستنزل عنها إلى مرتبة أخرى، بالمقاومة
والمناظرة: معاونة على النظر. ولو ألزم المعلل ذلك: لألزم بيان السلامة عن
المعارضة، وللزمه السير، ولكان يجب أن لا يبقى للخصم كلاما، فيقسم ويقول:
[نعارضه بكذا]، والكلام عليه لا يخلو إما أن يكون كيثت وكيت. فيأخذ في
إبطاله؛ [ثم أدلة إبطاله] أيضا - تفتقر إلى أنواع من السير؛ ويتسلسل إلى
غير ضبط.
وقد كان - من عادة القاضي في المناظرة - ذلك: فكان يستقصي - في أول الأمر
- كل ما [كان] يتوهم تعلق الخصم به - بطريق [46 - ب] السير - ويبطله: بحيث
لا يبقى للخصم متعلقا.
وهذا بعيد عن مصلحة المناظرة؛ اتفق المناظرون على خلافه.
فإذا بطل هذا المسلك، استقر قدم المعلل في دعواه: أن الوصف الذي ظهر
حدوثه، هو العلامة على العلة أو [هو] العلة. وعلى الخصم أن يشير إلى وصف
آخر، إن كان عنده، حتى يتكلم عليه.
فهذا بيان إحدى الدعويين، وهو: أن الوصف الحادث علامة أو PageV01P295 # علة، وكلاهما في الغرض واحد، فيكتفي من العلل بأن يستدل على كونه علة:
بحدوث الحكم عقب حدوثه. ويبطل عليه ملكه: بأن يبين [له] أنه حدث عقب وصف
آخر، حدث مع هذا الوصف: [مستقلا أو مضموما إليه]؛ فما الذي رجح أحدهما:
[على الآخر]؟، وعلى المجتهد البحث عن الأوصاف المقدرة الموهومة: التى تقدر
حادثة مع هذا الوصف مستقلا أو مضموما إليه.
فأما الدعوى الثانية - وهي المقصود بالإثبات -: أنه إذا سلم كونه علامة
أو علة، فما الذي يمنع اختصاصه بذلك المحل، فيقال: الشدة في ماء العنب
علامة، دون الشدة في غيره؟ وغاية ما في الباب أن يقال: لا مناسبة لهذا
التخصيص؛ وأصل العلة -[أيضا]- لا مناسبة له. فكيف الخلاص؟
فتقول: إذا سلم أن الحدوث عقب الوصف الحادث، دل على أن الوصف الحادث
علامة - فالعقول تثير إلى إتباع العلامات، والأعراض عن التخصيص بالمحال.
وهذا معلوم من تصرفات علماء PageV01P296 # الشرع، وهو راسخ في عقولهم - على وجه: يبعد إنكاره عنادا وجهلا [وغباوة].
فإن قيل: فلو أنكر منكر إشارة العقل إلى هذا، فليس يبقى بأيديكم إلا
التثبيت والإنكار، مع العجز عن إقامة دليل يهتدي به.
قلنا: المنكر - في هذا المقام - تضرب له الأمثلة؛ حتى إذا أصغى واعترف:
اهتدى. فإن أبى وجحد: اختزى واعتزى إلى مخالفة علماء الأمة [ومناكرة من سلف
ومضى]، ونحن نضرب ثلاثة أمثلة: مثالا مقدرا، ومثالا من مذهب الشافعي،
ومثالا من مذهب أبي حنيفه:
أما المثال المقدر، فهو ما قدمناه: من أنه لو قيل للنبي - عليه السلام -
ماتت شاه، فهل تباع؟ فقال: لا؛ لفهم [منه] أن الموت علامة لتحريم البيع. إذ
كان يجوز بيعها قبل الموت، ولم يحدث الآن غير حلول الموت؛ فحكم بتحريم
البيع. ففهم أن الموت علامة؛ فلو ماتت بقرة أو ناقة: لأحكم بمثل هذا الحكم،
وهذا لا سيبل إلى جحده، ولم تعرف مناسبة الموت: إذ ما يتخيل فيه -: من
تعطيل المنافع [فقد] أبطلناه، وذكرنا أنه خيال. ولو قدر الاخبار عن وصف آخر
