chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ي-ن (ʿAyn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "specifying, determining, or fixing upon a particular thing" — the act of isolating one attribute from a set of possible candidates.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, taʿyīn refers to the jurist's determination of the operative attribute (waṣf) that serves as the ratio legis (ʿillah) for a ruling, distinct from mere lexical designation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "to appoint or designate"; here it is used technically for the mental act of selecting a causal attribute — a ḥaqīqah in juristic discourse, not metaphorical.
- Root: ن-ق-ح (Naqaḥa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To refine, purify, or prune" — removing extraneous elements to arrive at the essential core.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Tanqīḥ al-manāṭ is the methodological process of eliminating non-operative attributes to isolate the true cause — a recognized procedure in uṣūl.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used metaphorically here — the attribute-set is "pruned" like a branch, retaining only what is causally relevant.
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿAlla)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To give a reason or cause"; the ʿillah is that which necessitates or justifies a ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ʿillah in kalām and uṣūl is the effective cause — either munāsib (suitable, reason-based) or ʿalāmah (mere sign/indicator).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Distinguishes ḥaqīqah (true causal efficacy) from majāz (metaphorical attribution) — a central theme in this passage.
- Root: خ-ص-ص (Khaṣaṣa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To specify or particularize" — restricting a general ruling to a specific instance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Takhṣīṣ al-ḥukm bi'l-maḥall — the problematic claim that a ruling applies only to its original locus, which Ghazali refutes.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): In rhetoric, takhṣīṣ is a form of qaṣr (restriction); here it is the juristic error of confining a causal attribute to one case.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-ḥukm ʿalā al-waṣf (Attributing the ruling to the attribute) — Syntactically, when a ruling is predicated on a conditional or descriptive phrase, the predicate follows the attribute, not the subject's identity; this mirrors the juristic principle that the ḥukm follows the ʿillah, not the maḥall.
chapters.translation:
I say: The specification of an attribute from among the events [that coincide with the ruling], or the refinement of its totality — by eliminating some [attributes] and retaining others — all of this proceeds without [recourse to] suitability (munāsabah), and prior to discovering the suitable attribute. Most analogical rulings (al-aḥkām al-qiyāsiyyah) are of this kind: for they are rulings that arose with the arising of necessitating causes, where the inquiry concerned the specification of attributes from among the newly-arisen necessitants, or their refinement.

The upshot of this answer has returned to [the claim] that the question demanding the specification of the ruling to its locus (takhṣīṣ al-ḥukm bi'l-maḥall) is incumbent [upon the opponent], but its invalidity is shown by consensus (ijmāʿ). This is like another objection (muʿāraḍah) that resists the mentioned attribute — namely, that it is not suitable (munāsib) — for it is repelled by way of refutation (naqḍ) through consensus, or by some method of preponderance (tarjīḥ). And this proceeds both between the transitive attribute (al-waṣf al-mutaʿaddī) and the intransitive one (al-qāṣir).

Some have said: The transitive [attribute] is more worthy than the intransitive in [establishing] causes (al-ʿilal), and the one transitive to multiple branches is more worthy than the one transitive to a single branch; preponderance is achieved by mere transitivity (al-taʿaddiyah).

The second answer — and it is the chosen one — is that if something of what we mentioned in the first answer occurs — namely, consensus indicating the invalidity of specification — then it is manifest and clear, with no doubt in it. But that [consensus] is not a condition [for every case].

Indeed, a group made it a condition; for it is reported from Bishr al-Marīsī and a company that they said: It is not permissible to reason by analogy (qiyās) from a root (aṣl) merely upon the establishment of the general evidence permitting qiyās. Rather, a specific evidence must indicate that the root upon which the analogy is based is operative through a cause (maʿmūl bihi bi-ʿillah). For I — despite the evidence for the principle of qiyās — allow that among those roots there may be one that is not caused (muʿallal), but rather is specified by its own occasion (mukhassaṣ bi-mawridihi). Thus, evidence is required that the root is caused (muʿallal).

I know no basis for this doctrine except what I have mentioned: for when the specifying attribute (al-waṣf al-mukhassiṣ) equals the transitive attribute in its detachment from suitability (al-infikāk ʿan al-munāsabah), they counterbalance each other. Hence, evidence for transitivity is required.

If the proponent of this doctrine restricts his doctrine to this kind — namely, causation devoid of suitability — then he has a basis. And its basis is clear, as we have mentioned.

But if he extends it to cases where suitable meanings (al-maʿānī al-munāsibah) are manifest, and says: "It is possible that the Lawgiver observed the suitable [meaning] in a specific locus; therefore evidence of transitivity is required" — or says: "It is possible that this suitable [meaning] occurred coincidentally (ittifāqan)" — then he is weaker in this direction, and his derivation draws from the doctrine denying the very principle of qiyās. To this the deniers of qiyās pointed in their insistence on restriction (al-iqtiṣār).

In sum: This doctrine is not sound in all cases; so do not require evidence of consensus for transitivity. And if consensus does occur, it is the highest and clearest [proof]. But we say: When an attribute arises, and a ruling arises subsequent to it, its arising subsequent to its arising indicates that the newly-arisen attribute is its locus of attachment (manāṭuhu), and that the ruling follows the attribute, not the locus. Then, if the attribute is suitable, its designation as "cause" (ʿillah) becomes manifest. If it is not suitable, then the apparent [indication] is that the ruling is attributed to it. It is possible that one who understands "cause" as the suitable [attribute] would not call it a cause; and it is possible that one who understands "cause" as the mere sign (al-ʿalāmah) would call it a cause; and it is possible that one would apply the name "cause" to it metaphorically (majāzan), while [reserving] "cause" in its literal sense (ḥaqīqatan) for the suitable [attribute]. For the suitable [attribute] has its mode of efficacy (wajh taʾthīrihi) in the ruling known, whereas this [non-suitable attribute] has its mode of efficacy unknown. But we opine that it encompasses the suitable, maslaha-based meaning (al-maʿnā al-munāsib al-maṣlaḥī) which we have not uncovered. Thus, this attribute is a marker (amārah) of that maslaha which is hidden from us, and its sign (ʿalāmah). We opine that it does not detach from it in most cases, and it takes the rank of the mold and the vessel (al-qālib wa'l-ẓarf). So calling it a "cause" — by way of its encompassing the cause, in a metaphorical manner — is not far-fetched.

This disagreement reverts to mere nomenclature (al-tasmīyah). The uṣūliyyūn have explicitly stated this disagreement; and there is no benefit in it. For the signs (al-ʿalāmāt) erected by the Law are followed — whether they are suitable to what they signify or not. So rules should not be leveled upon [words]; rather, words should be leveled upon meanings.

Thus, when the upshot of the inquiry returns to [the conclusion] that the indicator (al-ʿalam) of the newly-arisen ruling is the newly-arisen attribute — whose arising appeared at the outset of the inquiry — and that the ruling follows the attribute, not the locus, then the attribution to the locus is dropped when the sign appears, just as it is dropped when suitability appears.

If someone says: "This is a narration of the doctrine — so what is your evidence for it?"

We say: The doctrine comprises two claims. In which of them is the dispute? — One: that the attribute whose arising is manifest is a sign (ʿalāmah). The other: that the ruling follows the sign, not the locus in which the sign appeared.

If we are disputed regarding our statement that the newly-arisen attribute is a sign, then its evidence is what preceded: namely, that its arising subsequent to its arising indicates it — just as in the case of linguistic attribution (al-iḍāfah al-lafẓiyyah), and just as in the case of the ruling of the Messenger — peace be upon him — upon the occurrence of a new event, with a new ruling.

The evidence for it is: If, for example, it were known that there is no event except the attribute we mentioned, then attribution to it would be necessary. For the very principle of causation and attribution is necessarily obligatory by its arising after it had not been; so it requires a cause (muḥdith) by which it is distinguished from what preceded the events. If it were not caused, then our statement that attribution is obligatory would be nullified. And this is intelligible. And if it were not caused by this [particular] event, then our statement that there is no event besides it would be nullified. This [holds] when it is known — by definitive inference (al-sayr al-qaṭʿī) — that there is no event besides it.

If it is not known, but is merely probable (maẓnūnan), then that suffices for the mujtahid. And the one who posits a cause (al-muʿallil) suffices by specifying an attribute of which he claims that no other appeared to him — until he is alerted to another attribute that appeared besides it, whereupon he must address it.

No demand is directed at him to say: "Why did you say there is no event besides what you mentioned? Perhaps an attribute occurred that was hidden from you." For if this door were opened in disputation (al-jidāl), the path of inquiry would never be closed. And this [same demand] would be directed at everyone who posits a suitable [attribute], and it would be said to him: "Do you concede the invalidity of your suitable cause if another cause appeared, more evidently suitable than what you claim?" — according to what is established: the impossibility of causing a ruling by two causes known through suitability. If he says "Yes," then it is said: "What assures you against the existence of a suitable [attribute] more evident and stronger than what you claim, which you have not uncovered?" Thus, this question is repelled in disputation.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr said: One must proceed through the causes (al-sayr ʿalā al-ʿilal) — namely, that he erect his cause and demonstrate the non-existence of everything besides it. And he extended this to the suitable [attribute] as well.

This is far-fetched regarding the disputant (al-mujādil), but applicable regarding the mujtahid. For upon the mujtahid is the completion of inquiry, so that fatwā becomes permissible for him. But upon the one who posits a cause is only the ascent of a rank among the ranks of inquiry, until he is brought down from it to another rank, through resistance and debate (al-muqāwamah wa'l-munāẓarah) — as an aid to inquiry. If the one who posits a cause were obligated to that, he would be obligated to demonstrate safety from objection (al-muʿāraḍah), and obligated to [full] progression (al-sayr), and it would be required that no speech remain for the opponent — so he would divide and say: "We object with such-and-such," and the discourse upon it would either be of this kind or that kind. Then he would proceed to refute it; then the evidences of its refutation would also require types of progression; and it would regress infinitely (yatasalsal) beyond control.

It was the habit of al-Qāḍī in disputation to do that: he would exhaust — at the outset — everything that the opponent might conceivably cling to, by way of progression, and refute it, such that no attachment remained for the opponent.

This is far from the interest of disputation; the disputants have agreed upon its contrary.

When this path is nullified, the foot of the one who posits a cause is established in his claim that the attribute whose arising appeared is the sign of the cause, or is itself the cause. And upon the opponent is to point to another attribute, if he has one, so that he may address it.

This is the elucidation of one of the two claims — namely, that the newly-arisen attribute is a sign or a cause; and both are one in purpose. So the one who posits a cause suffices by adducing, for its being a cause, the arising of the ruling subsequent to its arising. And his opponent's possession [of the claim] is nullified by showing that [the ruling] arose subsequent to another attribute that arose with this attribute — either independently or conjoined with it. So what preponderates one over the other? And upon the mujtahid is the investigation of the estimated, conjectured attributes that might be estimated as arising with this attribute, independently or conjoined.

As for the second claim — and it is the one intended for proof — namely: When it is conceded that it is a sign or a cause, what prevents its specification to that locus? So it is said: "The intensity (al-shiddah) in grape-juice is a sign, but not the intensity in other [liquids]?" The utmost in this matter is to say: "There is no suitability for this specification; and the root of the cause — also — has no suitability for it. So how is the escape?"

So we say: When it is conceded that the arising subsequent to the newly-arisen attribute indicates that the newly-arisen attribute is a sign — then the intellects (al-ʿuqūl) impel toward following the signs, and turning away from specification to loci. And this is known from the practices of the scholars of the Law, and it is firmly rooted in their intellects — in a manner whose denial is far-fetched, whether out of obstinacy, ignorance, or stupidity.

If it is said: "If a denier denied the intellect's indication to this, then nothing remains in your hands except assertion and denial, along with incapacity to establish an evidence by which one might be guided."

We say: The denier — in this station — is given examples; until, when he listens and concedes, he is guided. If he refuses and denies, he is disgraced and retreats to opposing the scholars of the ummah and contending with those who have passed and gone before. And we shall give three examples: an estimated example, an example from the doctrine of al-Shāfiʿī, and an example from the doctrine of Abū Ḥanīfah.

As for the estimated example, it is what we have already presented: namely, that if it were said to the Prophet — peace be upon him — "A sheep has died; may it be sold?" and he said "No" — then it is understood from him that death is a sign for the prohibition of sale. For it was permissible to sell it before death, and nothing new occurred now except the arrival of death; so he ruled the prohibition of sale. Thus, it is understood that death is a sign. So if a cow or a camel had died, he would have ruled with the like of this ruling. There is no way to deny this. And no suitability for death is known — for what might be imagined in it, namely the nullification of benefits (taʿṭīl al-manāfiʿ), we have already refuted, and mentioned that it is a mere fancy. And if it were supposed that another attribute had arisen [alongside death]...

chapters.title_en: Clarifying the Meaning of the Statement: "It Is in the Meaning of the Original (Aṣl)"
chapters.arabic_text: ### ||| CHECK بيان معنى القول: أنه في معنى الأصل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ص-ل (A-ṣ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of "root, foundation, origin" — that from which something branches (farʿ) and to which it returns; the stable base of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, al-aṣl denotes the primary textual or rational source (e.g., Qurʾān, Sunnah, or consensus) from which a derivative ruling (farʿ) is analogically drawn; also the original state of a matter before alteration.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is "the lower part of a tree" or "foundation of a wall"; metaphorically (majāz), it applies to any principle or source that supports a branch — here, the "meaning" (maʿnā) that unites the original and the branch in legal causality (ʿillah).
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-Jumlah (Elliptical Clause Reconstruction) — The phrase "أنه في معنى الأصل" requires supplying an implicit predicate (e.g., "the branch is in the meaning of the original") to complete the syntactic sense, as the nominal sentence is elided.
chapters.translation: I say: Know that the statement "it is in the meaning of the original (aṣl)" is a technical expression whose intended sense must be clarified, for its ambiguity has led many astray in the science of legal causality (ʿillah). When the jurist says that a certain branch (farʿ) is "in the meaning of the original," he does not mean that the branch is identical to the original in every respect, nor that it shares the same textual wording (lafẓ). Rather, he means that the branch shares with the original a common effective attribute (maʿnā muʾaththir) — that is, the ratio legis (ʿillah) — by virtue of which the ruling of the original is extended to the branch. This shared meaning is not the original itself, nor is it a separate entity; rather, it is the very attribute that the Lawgiver (al-Shāriʿ) has made the cause of the ruling in the original, and which is found equally in the branch. Thus, the expression "in the meaning of the original" signifies that the branch is subsumed under the original's ruling because of the presence of that same effective meaning, not because of a mere verbal resemblance or a superficial analogy. And this is the precise sense intended by the scholars of uṣūl al-fiqh when they employ this phrase in the context of qiyās (analogical reasoning).

chapters.title_en: The Pursuit of Indicators Beyond the Locus of Occasioning Attributes
chapters.arabic_text:
أبعد من هذا الوصف؛ لكان الحكم عند حدوث ذلك الوصف مفهوما إضافته إلى ذلك
الوصف، وكون الوصف علامة عليه: حتى تقدر مشاركة البقرة والناقة للشاة فيها؛
وإن أنكر منكر  هذا، كان متأكدا، وإن زعم أنه من قبيل ما في معنى الأصل؛
قلنا: هذه عبارة اشتهرت، فلابد من البحث عنها. فإن قنع بمثل هذه العبارة،
فنحن نقول: الشدة [المطربة] لا تناسب - مثلا -[وهي] علة أو علامة، وشدة
نبيذ التمر كشدته وفي معناه. فلا تعجز عن إطلاق هذه العبارة في جميع
المواضع. ومعنى قولنا: في معناه؛ أنه شاركه فيما عرف كونه علة أو علامة؛
وأنه إنما فارقه فيما ليس له مدخل في العلامة، وهو: كونه شاة، وكونه بقرة.
وهذا لا مدخل له؛ فكان يمكن أن يقال، العلامة والعلة هو: الموت في الشاة،
كما يقول: هو الشدة في عصير العنب.
هذا هو المثال المقدر، وهو واضح. وفي تقرير أمثاله متسع؛ وهو: كل وصف
حادث رتب الشارع عليه حكما، والوصف الحادث لا يناسب الحكم.
المثال الثاني - من مذهب الشافعي - قوله: أن بيع العنب [بالعنب رطبا]
كيلا بكيل باطل؛ لأنه يتوقع نقصانه عند الجفاف: فصار PageV01P298 # كالرطب.
فقيل: ولم قلت: أن توقع النقصان في ثاني الحال علة الأبطال، مع حصول
التماثل في الحال؟ وهل هذا إلا تعليل بما لا يناسب؟
فقال: الدليل علي إثبات الوصف في الأصل، قوله - عليه السلام - للسائل:
"أينقص الرطب إذا جف"؟ فقال: نعم، فقال: "فلا إذن". فعلل بالنقصان عند
الجفاف.
فلو قيل [له]: علل بنقصان الرطب عند الجفاف، فلم عدت إلى العنب؟ - فلا
يمكنه الانفصال بإظهار المناسبة: إذ لا مناسبة، وإنما فهم الحكم، وفهم
علامة الحكم، وهو: توقع النقصان؛ فكان الحكم - مع العلامة - غير مخصوص [47
- أ] بمحل العلامة. فمتى تصرف في اللبن واللحمان وجميع الأشياء الرطبة،
وقدر لجميعها حالة الكمال - اعتبر التماثل بالإضافة إليها.
PageV01P299
ومن عرف مسالك المناسبة على ما قدمناه، عرف أنه لا مطمع في المناسبة في
هذه المسألة؛ ولكن اتبع العلامة كما اتبع العلة المناسبة. والعلل المناسبات
- عند التحقيق - علامات: فإنها لا توجب الأحكام لذواتها.
فإن قيل: ليس هذا وزان مسئلتكم؛ فإنه تلقى التعليل من الإضافة والإيماء
من جهة الشارع، لا من جهة الحدوث.
[قلنا]: ولسنا نورد هذا  المثال دليلا على أن الحدوث عقيب الوصف علامة
التعليل؛ وإنما أوردناه دليلا على من سلم أنه عرف بالحدوث عقيبه كونه
علامة، بالدليل الذي سبق؛ [ولكن] قال: هو علامة في هذا المحل حتى لا يتعدى.
ولا يستنكر هذا لعدم المناسبة في التخصيص، كما لم يستنكر لعدم المناسبة في
الأصل، وفي هذا لا يختلف الأمر باختلاف طرق معرفة العلامة؛ فالنقصان عرف
كونه علامة بالإيماء، وهو - بعد كونه علامة - لا يختص بالمحل، فكذلك الوصف:
إذا عرف كونه علامة بالحدوث عقيبه، لا يختص بالمحل وإن لم يناسب.
على أن الشافعي كيف يتعلق في التعدية بالإضافة، والإضافة إلى نقصان
الرطب، إذ قال: أينقص الرطب إذا جف، فنقصان العنب كيف صار علامة؟ فدل أن
العنب كالرطب محل العلامة، والحكم يتبع العلامة؛ وكذلك القول في الشدة التي
لا تناسب مثلا، هي بالنسبة إلى عصير الرطب، كهي بالنسبة إلى عصير العنب،
والموت بالنسبة إلى الشاة، كهو بالنسبة إلى البقرة وسائر الحيوانات.
PageV01P300
وبهذا، يتبين اتفاق العلماء على إتباع العلامات دون المحال.
المثال الثالث: قول أبي حنيفة: الجص مكيل، فيحرم فيه ربا الفضل كالبر؛
فطولب به، فقال: ظهر تأثير الكيل في ربا الفضل. قلنا: وما معنى تأثيره؟
قال: ظهور الحكم به، ومظهر الحكم علة الحكم. وهذا [منه] دليل على تسمية
العلامة علة: لأن العلامة تظهر كالعلة.
قال: ووجهه أن الفضل - الذي لا مقابل له - حرام في البيع بالاتفاق؛ وهو
أن يقول: بعتك هذا العبد بهذا الثوب، على أن تزيد درهما؛ فالدرهم فضل لا مقابل
له، فهو حرام، وإنما صار فضلا: بأن صارت المقابلة بحكم الشرط والصيغة،
مقصودة على العبد والثوب.
والشرع شرط المماثلة في مقابلة البر بالبر؛ فكانت الزيادة فضلا على
المثال: لا مقابل له بحكم الشرع. وإنما يصير فضلا على المثل، بحصول
المماثلة. وإنما تحصل المماثلة في القدر: بالكيل؛ وفي المعنى: بالجنسية،
فالعلة مركبة منهما؛ إذ بمجموعهما ظهر الفضل، وبظهور الفضل ظهر التحريم.
فسمي علة: لأنه مظهر [يظهر] الحكم. وهو الذي رددنا القول في تسمية جنسه علة
أو علامة  العلة.
والغرض: وراء هذا، وهو أن يقال له: هذه الأوصاف لا تناسب، وهي PageV01P301 # مظهرات. فإن سلم لك أنها العلامة، فهي علامة في الأشياء الستة؛ فلم
عديتها إلى غيرها: وأنت لا تطلع على وجه المناسبة فيها؟ فيقول: إذا سلم
[لي] أنها مظهرة، فهي علامة بنفسها حيث وجدت، ولا تختص بالمحال.
ومن سلم له كونه علامة لا ينازعه في الطرد، وإنما النزاع في طريق إثبات
كونه علامة؛ إذ يقال له: والبر المتهيء لحصول المماثلة فيه قدرا وجنسا، لم
شرط [الشرع] المماثلة الممكنة فيه؟ وبم عرفت [إن علامة الحكم] الإمكان؟
والمقصود أنه عدى الكيل والجنس، وهي علامة مظهرة، وليست علامة مناسبة أصلا.
فقد تبين - بالأمثلة من مذاهب العلماء - أن العلامة التي لا تناسب
[متبعة]، لا يجوز تخصيصها بالمحل، كالعلامة بالمناسبة. وإن المناسبة إحدى
الطرق التي يعرف بها كون الوصف علامة. وقد يعرف بغيرها: كالنص، والإيماء،
واستعقاب الحكم عند الحدوث، وجب عليه إتباع العلامة، وقطع النظر عن المحال،
وقد حصل بذلك دفع هذا السؤال [على أوضح وجه، للفطن المتأمل؛ إن شاء الله
تعالى].
PageV01P302
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿalima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Certain knowledge, perception of a thing’s essence; marking, signifying.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The sign (ʿalāmah) as that which discloses a ruling (ḥukm) without intrinsic causal efficacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a physical mark; metaphorical: any indicant (dalīl) that reveals a legal cause.
- Root: ح-د-ث (ḥadatha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Origination after non-existence; temporal contingency.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥudūth as the ontological marker of createdness, distinct from essential causality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: temporal occurrence; metaphorical: the epistemic clue that a ruling attaches to a novel attribute.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-ḥukm bi al-waṣf al-ḥādith (Attributing a ruling to a contingent attribute) — the conditional linkage of a legal judgment to a descriptive clause, parsed as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) rather than a causal agent.
chapters.translation:
I say: If the ruling were attached to the occurrence of that attribute, then the attribution of the ruling to that attribute would be understood, and the attribute’s being a sign (ʿalāmah) upon it — such that one could even posit the cow and the she-camel as sharing with the sheep in that ruling. And if anyone denies this, he is obstinate; and if he claims that it falls under the category of “what is in the meaning of the original” (mā fī maʿnā al-aṣl), we say: This is a phrase that has become widespread, and it must be investigated. For if he is content with such a phrase, then we say: The intoxicating intensity (al-shiddah al-muṭribah) — for example — does not suit (lā yunāsibu) [the ruling], whether it be a cause (ʿillah) or a sign; and the intensity of date-wine (nabīdh al-tamr) is like it and in its meaning. So you are not incapable of uttering this phrase in all contexts. And the meaning of our saying “in its meaning” is that it shares with it in what is known to be a cause or a sign; and that it only differs from it in what has no entry into the sign, namely: its being a sheep, and its being a cow. And this has no entry [into the sign]; so it could be said: The sign and the cause is death in the sheep, just as one says: It is the intensity in grape-juice.

This is the estimated example, and it is clear. And in establishing its likes there is ample scope; and it is: every contingent attribute (waṣf ḥādith) upon which the Lawgiver has ordered a ruling, while the contingent attribute does not suit the ruling.

The second example — from the school of al-Shāfiʿī — is his saying: The sale of fresh grapes (ʿinab) [by fresh grapes] by measure (kayl) is void; because diminution is anticipated for it upon drying: so it became like fresh dates (rutab). So it was said to him: Why did you say that the anticipation of diminution in the second state is the cause of invalidation, despite the attainment of equivalence (tamāthul) in the present state? And is this not merely an occasioning by what does not suit? He said: The proof for establishing the attribute in the original is his saying — peace be upon him — to the questioner: “Does the fresh date diminish when it dries?” He said: Yes. He said: “Then no [sale].” So he occasioned by the diminution upon drying.

Now if it were said to him: You occasioned by the diminution of the fresh date upon drying — so why did you transfer to the grape? — He cannot extricate himself by displaying suitability (munāsabah), for there is no suitability. Rather, he understood the ruling, and understood the sign of the ruling, namely: the anticipation of diminution. So the ruling — along with the sign — is not restricted to the locus of the sign. Thus whenever one deals with milk, meats, and all moist things, and posits for all of them a state of completion, equivalence is considered in relation to them.

And whoever knows the pathways of suitability (masālik al-munāsabah) as we have set forth, knows that there is no hope for suitability in this question; but the sign is followed just as the suitable cause is followed. And the suitable causes — upon verification — are signs: for they do not necessitate rulings by their own essences.

If it is said: This is not the measure of your question; for he received the occasioning from the indication (al-iḍāfah) and the gesture (al-īmāʾ) on the part of the Lawgiver, not from the aspect of contingency (al-ḥudūth). We say: And we do not adduce this example as proof that contingency upon the attribute is a sign of occasioning; rather, we adduce it as proof against one who conceded that he knew by the contingency upon it that it is a sign, by the proof that preceded; but he said: It is a sign in this locus so that it does not extend beyond it. And this is not deemed objectionable for the lack of suitability in the specification, just as it was not deemed objectionable for the lack of suitability in the original. And in this, the matter does not differ with the difference of the pathways of knowing the sign; for the diminution was known to be a sign by the gesture, and it — after being a sign — is not restricted to the locus. Likewise the attribute: when it is known to be a sign by the contingency upon it, it is not restricted to the locus, even if it does not suit.

Moreover, how would al-Shāfiʿī cling to the transfer by the indication, and the indication to the diminution of the fresh date, when he said: “Does the fresh date diminish when it dries?” — so how did the diminution of the grape become a sign? Thus it is shown that the grape is like the fresh date as a locus of the sign, and the ruling follows the sign. And likewise the saying concerning the intensity that does not suit, for example: it is in relation to grape-juice as it is in relation to date-juice; and death in relation to the sheep is as it is in relation to the cow and all other animals.

And by this, the agreement of the scholars upon following the signs, without [restricting to] the loci, becomes evident.

The third example: The saying of Abū Ḥanīfah: Gypsum (al-jiṣṣ) is measured (makīl), so the excess in exchange (ribā al-faḍl) is prohibited in it, like wheat. So he was pressed on it, and he said: The effect (athar) of measuring appeared in ribā al-faḍl. We say: And what is the meaning of its effect? He said: The appearance of the ruling by it; and the apparenter of the ruling is the cause of the ruling. And this — from him — is evidence for naming the sign a cause: because the sign appears like the cause.

He said: And its face is that the excess (al-faḍl) — which has no counterpart — is prohibited in the sale by consensus; and it is that one says: I sold you this slave for this garment, on condition that you add a dirham; so the dirham is an excess with no counterpart, and it is prohibited. And it only became excess by the fact that the counter-valuation (al-muqābalah), by virtue of the condition and the formula, became intended upon the slave and the garment. And the Law stipulated equivalence in the exchange of wheat for wheat; so the increase became an excess upon the like, with no counterpart by virtue of the Law. And it only becomes an excess upon the like by the attainment of equivalence. And equivalence is attained in quantity by measuring; and in meaning by generic identity (al-jinsiyyah). So the cause is composite of the two; for by their conjunction the excess appears, and by the appearance of the excess the prohibition appears. So it was named a cause because it is an apparenter that appears the ruling. And this is what we have debated concerning the naming of its genus as a cause or a sign of the cause.

And the purpose lies beyond this, namely: that it be said to him: These attributes do not suit, and they are appearers (muẓhirāt). If you concede that they are the sign, then they are a sign in the six [commodities]; so why did you transfer them to others — while you do not discern the face of suitability in them? He would say: If it is conceded to me that they are appearers, then they are a sign by themselves wherever they are found, and they are not restricted to the loci. And whoever concedes to him that it is a sign does not dispute him on the extension (al-ṭard); rather, the dispute is only in the pathway of establishing that it is a sign; for it is said to him: And wheat, which is prepared for the attainment of equivalence in it in quantity and genus — why did the Law stipulate the possible equivalence in it? And by what did you know that possibility is the sign of the ruling? And the point is that he extended the measuring and the generic identity, and they are an appearing sign, and they are not a suitable sign at all.

So it has become evident — by the examples from the schools of the scholars — that the sign which does not suit is followed, and it is not permissible to restrict it to the locus, like the sign by suitability. And that suitability is one of the pathways by which an attribute is known to be a sign. And it may be known by other than it: such as the text (al-naṣṣ), the gesture (al-īmāʾ), and the entailment of the ruling upon contingency (istiʿqāb al-ḥukm ʿinda al-ḥudūth). So it is incumbent upon him to follow the sign, and to cut off consideration from the loci. And by this, the repulsion of this question has been achieved in the clearest manner, for the discerning and contemplative one — if God — exalted — wills.

chapters.title_en: The Discourse on Analogy of Resemblance (Qiyās al-Shabah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| AUTO القول في

### || AUTO قياس الشبه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ب ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "resemblance" or "similarity" between two things in attributes or states, often implying a partial or apparent likeness rather than identity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, al-shabah denotes a shared attribute (ʿillah) that is not explicitly stated in the revealed text but is inferred from a common descriptive feature, serving as a basis for extending a ruling (ḥukm) from an original case (aṣl) to a new case (farʿ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) refers to visible or conceptual resemblance; metaphorical usage (majāz) extends to juridical analogy where the resemblance is in the ratio legis (ʿillah), not in the outward form.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʾIḍāfah (Genitive Construction) — The phrase "qiyās al-shabah" is an annexation where the first term (qiyās) is defined by the second (al-shabah), indicating a specific type of analogy, not analogy in general.
chapters.translation: I say: Now we turn to the discourse on the analogy of resemblance (qiyās al-shabah). This is the form of analogical reasoning wherein the common cause (ʿillah) is not derived from an explicit textual indication (naṣṣ) or a consensus (ijmāʿ), but rather from a shared descriptive attribute that unites the original case (aṣl) and the branch case (farʿ) in a manner that the mind perceives as suitable for the ruling, though not decisively so. Its validity rests on the preponderance of resemblance over dissimilarity, and its application is confined to cases where no stronger indicator (dalīl) from the Book, the Sunnah, or consensus opposes it.

chapters.title_en: The Completion of the Exposition of Co-Extensiveness and Co-Exclusiveness (al-Ṭard wa al-ʿAks)
chapters.arabic_text:
وفيه تمام بيان الطرد [47 - ب]
فإن قيل: حاصل معتصمكم في التعلق بالطرد والعكس، يرجع إلى التعلق بأن لا
متجدد إلا الوصف الحادث، وقد كان الحكم معدوما قبل، ووجد الآن، ولا فارق
بين الحالتين المفترقتين في الحكم، إلا الوصف الحادث، فكان الوصف الفارق
مناطا للفرق بين الحالتين، وعلامة على الحكم المتجدد، وهذا في وصف يعترى
على ذات واحدة، فكان الوصف فارقا بين الحالتين.
ويلزمكم- على مساق القول به- الحكم بأن الفارق بين الذاتين، المفترقتين
في الحكم علامة الافتراق: إذا لم يظهر فارق سواه، وإن لم يكن مناسبا. فإن
ظهر فارق آخر: قابله، إلى أن يترجح عليه، كما في الوصف الحادث الفارق بين
حالتي الذات الواحدة.
وبيانه: أنه لو قدر الخمر المشتد مائعا بنفسه، غير [متصف بالعصير]،
والخل، بل كانت الشدة وصفا مساوقا لوجوده، وورد PageV01P303 # الشرع بتحريمه وتحليل الخل والعصير والأدهان، لأمكن أن يقال: [لا فارق]
بينه وبين  سائر المائعات إلا الشدة، فلتكن الشدة علامة، حتى يتعدى إلى مشتد
آخر هو: نبيذ التمر مثلا، فهذا مثال مقدر.
ونذكر مثالا واقعا، وهو: أن التكرار مشروع في غسل الأعضاء وفاقا، وغير
مشروع في المسح على الخف وفاقا، فإذا نظر الناظر إليه: لم يتميز المسح عن
الغسل إلا بكونه مسحا، وإلا فهو ركن في الطهارة، وجار مجراه في كل قضية إلا
في كونه مسحا. فليكن كونه مسحا علامة ترك التكرار، حتى يتعدى إلى مسح
الرأس، وهو متنازع فيه. وإذا قيل بذلك، يقابله أن الغسل شرع فيه التكرار،
وتميز عن المسح على الخف بكونه أصلا: لا مدخل للبدل فيه، فيتعدى إلى مسح
الرأس، فتصح كل واحدة من العلتين، إلى أن يظهر الترجيح.
وكذلك يقول الحنفي، لا ربا في الثياب والعبيد، وجرى في الأشياء الستة،
ولا تفارقها إلا في كونها مقدرة. فهو العلامة، وتتعدى إلى المقدرات.
والمالكي يقول: [بل] خالف الأشياء الأربعة غيرها من العبيد والثياب، في
كونها قوتا، فهو العلة والعلامة.
والشافعي يقول: لا، بل فارق في كونها مطعوما.
PageV01P304
وتتقاوم هذه الأوصاف، فيقضي بأن كل واحد صالح، فلابد من الترجيح
والامتحان الشواهد. ولو فتح هذا الباب: لا تسع النطاق في القياس، ولأمكن
التعليل بكل وصف مطرد غير منتقض.
فإن قلتم بذلك: كنتم محدثين أمرا بدعا بين المحققين من العلماء، وانغمستم
في غمار الحشوية من الطردية.
PageV01P305
وإن أبيتم ذلك: لم تجدوا فرقا وفصلا بين هذه الرتبة، وبين الطرد والعكس
الذي قدمتوه. فإن ذلك [يرجع حاصله إلى إضافة الافتراق في الحكم، إلى وصف
فارق بين حالتي ذات واحدة، وهذا] رجع حاصله إلى إضافة الافتراق في الحكم،
إلى وصف فارق بين ذاتين متعددتين، ولا فرق بين المقامين. وكيف يعتقد بينهما
فرق مع تقاربهما؟ وأي فرق بين أن نعلم أن الكلب محرم بيعه مثلا، فيقول
قائل: بيع سائر الحيوانات دون الكلب جائز، فكان السبب كونه كلبا: فإنه
الفارق. وكان هذا كما لو تصور أن يصير حيوان- ليس كلبا- بالانقلاب كلبا،
لكنا نقول: قبل الانقلاب يباع، وبعده لا يباع،  ولم يحدث إلا وصف الكلبية،
كما لم يحدث- في انقلاب العصير- إلا وصف الخمرية والشدة. فلا مدرك للفرق
بين المقامين وفيه فتح باب الطرد والانسلال عن ضبط المعنى المناسب المؤثر،
وذلك لا وجه له؟
[قلنا]: هذا إلزام للقول بالشبه، وهو: الوصف الذي لا يناسب، ويظن كونه
علامة متضمنة للعلة التي غابت عنا، فيحكم بالاشتراك في الحكم، عند الاشتراك
فيه.
PageV01P306
والقول به تلو القول بالطرد والعكس- كما سبق- إلزامه علة، والقول بالطرد
والعكس هو [تلو] القول بإضافة [الأحكام إلى الأسباب] الواقعة الحادثة،
[التي يترتب] جواب الشارع عليها، والقول به [هو تلو] القول بإضافة الأحكام
إلى الأسباب، باللفظ: بفاء التعقيب، وصيغة الشرط، والصفة الفارقة. كما
ضربناه: من الأمثلة في مسلك الإيماء. والقول بجميع ذلك، تلو القول بالتصريح
بالتعليل. والمناسبة غير مشروطة في شيء من هذه المراتب.
ومن قال بالأول، لزمه القول بما يليه: بحيث لا نجد بين الرتبتين فرقا،
وينحط إلى رتبة [48 - أ] الطرد: فيلزمه القول بالطرد. ونعني بالطرد: الوصف
الذي لا يناسب.
ومن أنكر الطرد: يلزمه إنكار الشبه، فإنه عين الطرد كما سنذكره، ومن
أنكرهما: لزمه إنكار الطرد والعكس، والحدوث PageV01P307 # عند حدوث الوصف، وترتيب الحكم على جواب الواقعة، وهلم جرا إلى المراتب
التي قبلها، حتى ينكر الدرجة العليا في الظهور، وهو: صريح التعليل.
فإذا قال الشارع مثلا: اقتلوا هذا لأنه أسود، فيقول هذا القائل: لا يتبع
السواد في شخص آخر، بل يختص [ذلك] الحكم بذلك الشخص، وقد انجر القول إلى
هذا الحد بمنكري القياس، وهو اللازم على مساق إنكار [القول بالطرد]، وانجر
القول بالقائمين إلى القول بالطرد، وهو اللازم على مساق القول بالقياس.
والوقوف على مرتبة من المراتب تحكم محض، مستنده: قصور [النظر عن الوقوف
على] [وجه] إلزام رتبة على رتبة، وكيفية ترتيب درجة على درجة، وهذه هي
المغاصة الكبرى، والمحارة العظمى، لعقول المتصرفين، وإنما الرجل: من يرتقي
من هذه المغاصة.
فإن قال قائل: هذا قول منكم بتكافي الأدلة، ورد على جميع أهل الملة،
فإنكم أبطلتم الوقوف على مرتبة: لاستحالة الفرق، وأبطلتم إنكار الطرد:  فإنه
يتداعى إلى إنكار صريح التعليل، وأبطلتم
PageV01P308
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ر-د (ṭ-r-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Continuous pursuit, driving forth; a description that co-extends with the ruling without exception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A non-appropriateness-based attribute used as a mere indicator (ʿalāmah) of a legal cause, lacking intrinsic suitability (munāsabah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is 'chasing away'; metaphorically, it denotes the unbroken concomitance of a descriptor with a judgment, without causal insight.
- Root: ش-ب-ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance, ambiguity; a descriptor that is not suitable (munāsib) but is presumed to be a sign of a hidden cause.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The "shabah" (semblance) is a middle rank between ṭard and explicit causation—an attribute whose suitability is unknown, yet it is treated as a marker.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Metaphorical extension of 'likeness' to legal inference, where the attribute is not known to be appropriate but is taken as a clue.
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Recurring cause, defect; the effective attribute (ʿillah) that necessitates a ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The true cause must be munāsib (appropriate); without it, inference collapses into ṭard.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal 'sickness' or 'second watering'; technically, the ratio legis that justifies a legal norm.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Concomitance (al-Talāzum al-Sharṭī) — The syntactic structure "if X, then Y" (law... la-kāna) governs the hypothetical examples, where the protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) are strictly correlated, mirroring the legal inference from a descriptor to a ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: This section completes the exposition of co-extensiveness (al-ṭard).

If it is said: The sum of your reliance on co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness reduces to this: that nothing is newly originated (ḥādith) except the newly occurring descriptor (al-waṣf al-ḥādith). The ruling was non-existent before, and now it exists; and there is no differentiator (fāriq) between the two distinct states in respect of the ruling except that newly occurring descriptor. Thus, the differentiating descriptor becomes the locus of attachment (manāṭ) for the difference between the two states, and a sign (ʿalāmah) of the newly originated ruling. This applies to a descriptor that supervenes upon a single essence (dhāt wāḥidah), so the descriptor is a differentiator between the two states.

And it necessarily follows for you—on the course of affirming this—that you must judge that the differentiator between two essences (dhātayn) that are distinct in respect of the ruling is a sign of their divergence, when no other differentiator appears besides it, even if it is not appropriate (munāsib). But if another differentiator appears, it confronts it, until one outweighs the other, just as in the case of the newly occurring descriptor that differentiates between the two states of a single essence.

Its clarification: Suppose that intoxicating wine (al-khamr al-mushtadd) were a liquid by itself, not characterized by being juice (ʿaṣīr) or vinegar (khall), but rather the intensity (al-shiddah) were a descriptor coeval with its existence; and the Lawgiver (al-sharʿ) had prohibited it and permitted vinegar, juice, and oils—then it could be said: There is no differentiator between it and the other liquids except the intensity. So let the intensity be the sign, such that it extends to another intense substance, namely, date-wine (nabīdh al-tamr), for example. This is a hypothetical example.

And we mention an actual example: Repetition (al-takrār) is legislated in washing the limbs (ghasl al-aʿḍāʾ) by consensus, and it is not legislated in wiping over the leather socks (al-masḥ ʿalā al-khuff) by consensus. When the observer looks at this, wiping is not distinguished from washing except by its being wiping (masḥ); otherwise, it is a pillar (rukn) in purification and runs its course in every matter, except in its being wiping. So let its being wiping be the sign of omitting repetition, such that it extends to wiping the head (masḥ al-raʾs), which is disputed. And if this is said, it is confronted by the fact that repetition is legislated in washing, and it is distinguished from wiping over the socks by its being an original (aṣl) in which substitution (badal) has no entry—so it extends to wiping the head. Thus, each of the two causes (ʿillatayn) becomes valid, until a preponderance (tarjīḥ) appears.

Likewise, the Ḥanafī says: There is no ribā (usury) in garments (thiyāb) and slaves (ʿabīd), and it applies to the six commodities (al-ashyāʾ al-sittah), and they are not distinguished from them except by their being measured (muqaddarah). So that is the sign, and it extends to all measured things.

The Mālikī says: Rather, the four commodities differ from others—slaves and garments—in their being sustenance (qūt). So that is the cause and the sign.

The Shāfiʿī says: No, rather they differ in their being edible (maṭʿūm).

These descriptors confront one another, and it is judged that each one is valid (ṣāliḥ). Thus, preponderance and examination of evidences (shawāhid) are necessary. If this door were opened, the scope of analogical reasoning (al-qiyās) would not contain it, and it would be possible to posit a cause for every co-extensive, non-refuted descriptor.

If you affirm this, then you have introduced an unprecedented matter (amran bidaʿan) among the verifiers (al-muḥaqqiqīn) of the scholars, and you have plunged into the ranks of the vulgar traditionalists (al-Ḥashwiyyah) among the proponents of co-extensiveness.

And if you refuse this, you will find no difference or distinction between this rank and the co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness that you have advanced. For the sum of that reduces to attributing the divergence in the ruling to a descriptor that differentiates between two states of a single essence; and this reduces to attributing the divergence in the ruling to a descriptor that differentiates between two multiple essences. There is no difference between the two positions. How can one believe there is a difference between them, given their proximity? And what difference is there between our knowing that the dog (al-kalb) is prohibited to sell, for example, such that one says: The sale of all other animals except the dog is permissible, so the cause was its being a dog, for it is the differentiator—and this is like imagining that an animal that is not a dog becomes a dog by transformation (inqilāb)? For we say: Before the transformation it is sold, and after it, it is not sold; and nothing new occurred except the attribute of dogness (al-kalbiyyah), just as nothing new occurred—in the transformation of juice—except the attribute of wine-ness (al-khamriyyah) and intensity. So there is no means of perceiving a difference between the two positions. And in this is the opening of the door of co-extensiveness and the slipping away from the control of the appropriate, effective meaning (al-maʿnā al-munāsib al-muʾaththir)—and that has no justification.

We say: This is an entailment (ilzām) of affirming the semblance (al-shabah), which is the descriptor that is not appropriate, yet is thought to be a sign containing the cause that is hidden from us; thus, one judges the sharing in the ruling upon the sharing in it.

Affirming it is a sequel to affirming co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness—as has preceded—and its entailment is a cause. Affirming co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness is a sequel to affirming the attribution of rulings to the occurring, newly originated causes (al-asbāb al-wāqiʿah al-ḥādithah), upon which the Lawgiver's response is ordered. And affirming that is a sequel to affirming the attribution of rulings to causes by verbal expression: by the particle of consequence (fāʾ al-taʿqīb), the conditional form (ṣīghat al-sharṭ), and the differentiating attribute (al-ṣifah al-fāriqah), as we have exemplified in the path of indication (maslak al-īmāʾ). And affirming all of that is a sequel to affirming explicit causation (al-taṣrīḥ bi al-taʿlīl). Appropriateness (al-munāsabah) is not a condition in any of these ranks.

Whoever affirms the first is necessarily compelled to affirm what follows it, such that we find no difference between the two ranks; and he descends to the rank of co-extensiveness—so he must affirm co-extensiveness. By co-extensiveness (al-ṭard) we mean: the descriptor that is not appropriate.

Whoever denies co-extensiveness must deny the semblance (al-shabah), for it is the very same as co-extensiveness, as we shall mention. Whoever denies both must deny co-extensiveness-and-co-exclusiveness, and the origination (al-ḥudūth) of the ruling upon the origination of the descriptor, and the ordering of the ruling upon the response to the event (jawāb al-wāqiʿah), and so on down to the ranks before them, until he denies the highest degree in evidentness (al-ẓuhūr), which is explicit causation.

Thus, if the Lawgiver says, for example: "Kill this one because he is black," and this speaker says: Blackness is not followed in another person; rather, that ruling is specific to that person—then the discourse has been dragged to this limit by the deniers of analogical reasoning (munkirū al-qiyās). This is what necessarily follows from denying co-extensiveness. And the discourse of those who affirm [analogy] is dragged to affirming co-extensiveness—this is what necessarily follows from affirming analogy.

Stopping at any one of these ranks is pure arbitrariness (taḥakkum maḥḍ), whose basis is the failure of consideration (qaṣūr al-naẓar) to perceive the manner of entailing one rank upon another, and the modality of ordering one degree upon another. This is the great whirlpool (al-maghāṣṣah al-kubrā) and the supreme pearl (al-muḥārah al-ʿuẓmā) for the minds of those who exercise independent judgment (al-mutaṣarrifīn). The true man is only he who ascends from this whirlpool.

If someone says: This is a statement from you affirming the equivalence of evidences (takāfuʾ al-adillah), and a refutation of all the people of the religious community (ahl al-millah). For you have nullified stopping at any rank, due to the impossibility of differentiation; and you have nullified the denial of co-extensiveness, for it collapses into denying explicit causation; and you have nullified...

chapters.title_en: The Verification of Its Authoritativeness and the Terminology of Imām al-Ḥaramayn and al-Dabbūsī Regarding It
chapters.arabic_text:
### ||| CHECK حجيته، وما كان يصطلح عليه إمام الحرمين والدبوسي فيه

القياس: لأنه ينجر إلى القول بالطرد، والقول بالطرد باطل، وما يلزم عليه
الباطل فهو باطل، فما سبيل الترقي عن هذه المهواة؟ ولابد من كشف الضمير،
وإبداء المعتقد [فيه].
قلنا: القول بالقياس حق، عرف ذلك- قطعا- من الشرع، وتصرف علماء الصحابة
وإجماعهم عليه، فكون أصل القياس حقا مقطوع به، وكل ما إلى إنكار القياس
الحق فهو باطل، وكل ما يلزم على القول بالقياس فهو حق، لأن القياس حق في
الشرع على القطع.
وعند هذا نبدي ما هو السر؟ فنقول: قياس الطرد صحيح، والمعنى به: التعليل
بالوصف الذي لا يناسب، على الحد الذي قدمناه في بيان المناسبات.
وعند هذا، ربما تنفر طباع بني الزمان عن سماع [مثل] هذا الكلام، لكثرة ما
قرع مسامعهم: من التشنيعات على الطردية وأصحابها. فيعتقد [به] السامع أن
هذا مذهب مبتدع خارج عن أقاويل أكابر العلماء، وأنه لا دليل عليه.
ونحن نقيم الدليل عليه، ونبين أنه مقول به عند أكابر العلماء: كالشافعي
وأبي حنيفة ومالك -رضي الله عنهم، ونبين أن المشنعين على أرباب PageV01P309 # الطرد- من علماء العصر القريب: كأبي زيد رحمه الله، وأستاذي إمام الحرمين
- رضي الله عنه - من القائلين به، إلا أن إمام الحرمين كان يعبر عن الطرد
الذي لا يناسب: بالشبه، ويقول: الطرد باطل، والشبه صحيح. وأبو زيد يعبر [عن
الطرد: بالمخيل، وعن الشبه: بالمؤثر] ويقول: المخيل باطل، والمؤثر صحيح،
وقد بينا بأمثلة: أنه [أراد] بالمؤثر ما أردناه بالمخيل.
وسنين بالأمثلة أن الذين قالوا بالشبه وأنكروا الطرد، فقد أرادوا بالشبه
ما أردنا بالطرد. وإنما انقسام الوصف إلى قسمين: مناسب كما ذكرناه وغير مناسب.
فالمناسب حجة وفاقا، ومنهم من لقبه: بالمؤثر، وأنكر المخيل. حتى ظن فريق
وقوع الاختلاف بين الجنسين، وإنما المختلف: العبارة لا المعنى.
وغير المناسب- أيضا- حجة: إذا دل عليه الدليل، وقد لقبه فريق: بالشبه،
حيث اضطروا إلى القول به. حتى يتخيل متخيل أن الشبه غير الطرد، والطرد غير
الشبه، ولو سئلوا عن  الفرق: اعترفوا بأنهم لا يحسبون بينهما فرقا محققا،
وإنما يرددون ألفاظا لا حاصل وراءها.
PageV01P310
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ر-د (ṭ-r-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is 'to drive away, expel, or chase' — indicating a description that is merely co-extensive with the ruling without any intrinsic suitability (munāsabah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, al-ṭard denotes a purely formal correlation between the attribute (waṣf) and the legal effect (ḥukm), lacking any rational or revealed indication of causality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical expulsion; metaphorically, it is the 'expulsion' of meaning from the attribute — i.e., stripping it of any evidentiary suitability.
- Root: ش-ب-ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance or similarity; in legal theory, it refers to an attribute that is not inherently suitable but is accepted as a valid ground for analogy due to external evidence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-shabah is a quasi-suitability — a semblance of appropriateness that, while not self-evidently causal, is elevated to validity by corroborating proof.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: likeness; metaphorical: a 'likeness' of the attribute to a true cause, without full identity.
- Root: خ-ي-ل (kh-y-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To imagine or fancy; al-mukhayyil is that which produces an illusion of suitability.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-mukhayyil is the attribute that appears suitable (munāsib) in form but is not genuinely so — a deceptive semblance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: causing imagination; metaphorical: the attribute 'imagines' causality without actual grounding.
- Root: أ-ث-ر (a-th-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To leave a trace or effect; al-muʾaththir is the attribute that truly effects the ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-muʾaththir is the genuinely suitable attribute (al-munāsib) that is agreed upon as a valid cause.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: leaving an imprint; metaphorical: the attribute 'imprints' the ruling, i.e., is its true cause.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Clauses (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The phrase "وما يلزم عليه الباطل فهو باطل" employs a conditional construction where the protasis (the entailment of falsehood) necessitates the apodosis (the falsehood of the antecedent), requiring precise parsing of the logical implication as a syntactic parallel.
chapters.translation:
I say: The verification of its authoritativeness, and what Imām al-Ḥaramayn and al-Dabbūsī were accustomed to terming therein.

Analogical reasoning (al-qiyās): because it drags one toward the doctrine of pure co-extension (al-ṭard), and the doctrine of pure co-extension is false, and whatever entails falsehood is itself false — so what is the path of ascent from this abyss? It is imperative to disclose the inner conviction and to reveal the belief held regarding it.

We say: The doctrine of analogical reasoning is true; this is known — definitively — from the Sacred Law, and from the practice of the scholars among the Companions and their consensus upon it. Thus, the fact that the principle of analogical reasoning is true is a matter of certainty, and everything that leads to the denial of true analogical reasoning is false, and whatever follows from affirming analogical reasoning is true, because analogical reasoning is true in the Sacred Law with certainty.

And at this point, we disclose what the secret is. We say: The analogy of pure co-extension (qiyās al-ṭard) is sound, and what is meant by it is: the act of rendering as a cause (al-taʿlīl) an attribute that possesses no suitability (munāsabah), according to the limit we have already set forth in the exposition of suitabilities.

And at this point, the temperaments of the people of this age may recoil from hearing such speech, due to the abundance of what has struck their ears — of the vilifications directed against the proponents of pure co-extension and their partisans. Thus, the listener comes to believe that this is an innovated doctrine, departing from the sayings of the great scholars, and that there is no proof for it.

But we shall establish the proof for it, and we shall show that it is a doctrine affirmed by the great scholars — such as al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah, and Mālik — may God be pleased with them all — and we shall show that those who vilify the partisans of pure co-extension — from the scholars of the recent era, such as Abū Zayd, may God have mercy on him, and my teacher Imām al-Ḥaramayn, may God be pleased with him — are themselves among those who affirm it, except that Imām al-Ḥaramayn used to express the pure co-extension that lacks suitability by the term 'resemblance' (al-shabah), and he would say: pure co-extension is false, but resemblance is sound. And Abū Zayd used to express pure co-extension by the term 'the illusory' (al-mukhayyil), and resemblance by the term 'the effective' (al-muʾaththir), and he would say: the illusory is false, but the effective is sound. And we have already shown by examples that by 'the effective' he meant what we meant by 'the illusory.'

And we have made clear by examples that those who affirmed 'resemblance' and denied 'pure co-extension' meant by 'resemblance' precisely what we meant by 'pure co-extension.' The division of the attribute into two categories is only this: suitable (munāsib) as we have mentioned, and non-suitable. So the suitable is a proof by agreement, and among them are those who labeled it 'the effective' and denied 'the illusory' — until a group fancied that a real difference occurred between the two kinds, when in fact what differed was only the expression, not the meaning.

And the non-suitable — also — is a proof, when a proof indicates it; and a group labeled it 'resemblance,' since they were compelled to affirm it. Until one might imagine that 'resemblance' is other than 'pure co-extension,' and 'pure co-extension' other than 'resemblance.' And were they asked about the difference, they would confess that they do not reckon between them any verified difference, and that they merely repeat words behind which there is no substance.

### ||| CHECK إختلاف المذاهب في الطرد والعكس والشبه

ونحن نكشف الغطاء عن هذه العمايات، وملتطم هذه العبارات، بضرب الأمثلة:
حتى يطلع الناظر على غور هذا الفصل، فلقد قل في [هذا] العصر من يستقل بفهم
هذا الكلام، فضلا عن درايته، والاستبداد بتقريره إلى نهايته. فنقول:
اختلفت المذاهب في الطرد والعكس والشبه، فمنهم: من قال بأحدهما دون
الآخر، ومنهم: من أنكرهما، ومنهم: من قال بهما. ونحن نقول:
مذهب الشافعي وأبي حنيفة ومالك-ي- القول بهما، فإنهم قالوا: بالشبه، وهو
أضعف من القول بالطرد والعكس.
ونحن نذكر الدليل، ثم [ننتقل إلى] الأمثلة، وبتقرير الأمثلة يتبين
الدليل، فإن الدليل على هذه الأمثلة: أن نبين أنها محصلة غلبة الظن، وذلك
يحصل بضرب المثال.
أما الدليل الجملي، فما ذكرناه في الطرد والعكس، وهو: تلوه، لأنا قد بينا
أن الوصف [48 - ب]- الفارق بين الحالتين في ذات واحدة- أوجب إضافة الافتراق
في الحكم إليه، لأنه هذا افتراق واقع لم يكن: فافتقر إلى علامة معرفة، وليس
ذلك إلا الوصف الظاهر. وعماد هذا الكلام أن لا يظهر وصف [آخر حادث] سوى ما
ذكر، PageV01P311 # وظهوره ممكن، وعلى المجتهد البحث عنه، وعلى المعلل الانتهاض لردة: إذا
ذكر، ولا شيء عليه قبل أن يذكر. فكذلك الفارق بين الذاتين: كالفارق بين
الحالتين في ذات واحدة.
فإذا قال الشارع: القاتل لا يرث، فهمنا أن القتل علامة الحرمان، ناسبت أو
لم تناسب، فإنه لو قال: الطويل لا يرث، والأسود لا يرث، لكنا نقول: الطول
والسواد علامة، وهما يتضمنان وجها في المصلحة لا نطلع عليه. ولو لم يرد هذا
اللفظ، ولكن عرف من الإجماع أنه لا يرث، أو حكم - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، في
شخص أخبر عن قتله، بأنه لا يرث- لكنا نفهم كون القتل علامة للفرق بين
الوارث وغير الوارث، بإضافته إلى شخص آخر: يساويه في القرابة، إذ يقال: لا
يفارقه إلا في كونه قاتلا، فهو المناط- كما يقال: لا تفارق حالة الشدة ما
قبلها، إلا في الشدة- وإن  احتمل أن يكون المناط معنى يتضمن القتل، ولكن ذلك
لا يمنع جعل القتل علامة، إلا أن يتبين متضمن له أولى بالاعتبار منه.
PageV01P312
والغرض: أن إضافة الحكم إلى شخص، كإضافة الحال إلى حال: في قضاء العقل
بإحالة الافتراق على الوصف الظاهر المفرق [أولا، وتتمة] هذا النظر: ببيان
أنه لا فارق سواه يجاور الوصف الظاهر، أو يتضمنه الوصف الظاهر.
وكذلك: إذا عرف أن الأسود لا يرث، فيعرف كون السواد علامة- بمقابلته
بالأبيض، كما يعرف ذلك بمقابلة بحالة سابقة- على ذلك الشخص بعينه- كان فيها أبيض.
وكذلك القول في الرق: يعرف كونه علامة الحرمان، بتقدير الطريان مرة على
شخص واحد، وبتقدير الإضافة إلى ذات حر.
فالفرق مطلوب بين الذاتين، كالفرق بين الحالتين، وإذا لم يكن بد من
الفارق- ولا فارق إلا الوصف الذي ادعاه المعلل-: فهو مناط الفرق: إن سلم
أنه لا فارق إلا ذلك، كما قررناه في الفارق بين الحالتين المتعاقبتين على
ذات واحدة يجرى- في حق المجتهد والمجادل المعلل- على ذلك المذاق بعينه،
فإنه [هو هو، ودليله دليله] وإنما يتضح وجه الدلالة، بضرب الأمثلة.

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ر-د (ṭarada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow in succession; to drive forth continuously — denoting an attribute that never departs from its subject (co-extensiveness).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, the property of a legal indicator (ʿalāmah) that accompanies the ruling in all cases without exception.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of sequential pursuit; metaphorically, the logical "running along" of a cause with its effect.
- Root: ع-ك-س (ʿakasa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To reverse, to turn back — signifying the converse relation (co-exclusiveness), i.e., the absence of the attribute entails absence of the ruling.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The reciprocal implication between cause and effect in legal reasoning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal inversion; technically, the test of whether the attribute is absent when the ruling is absent.
- Root: ش-ب-ه (shabaha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance, similarity between two things in some aspect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal "resemblance" (shabah) — an attribute that aligns the case with a comparable legal category due to a shared salient feature.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal likeness; in juristic method, a weaker form of causation than ṭard and ʿaks, as it relies on apparent similarity rather than necessary concomitance.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs "لو" (if) and "إلا" (except) to frame hypothetical legal scenarios, requiring precise parsing of the protasis and apodosis to isolate the operative attribute (al-waṣf al-muʾaththir).
chapters.translation:
I say: We shall lift the veil from these obscurities and disentangle the interwoven expressions by striking examples — so that the observer may penetrate to the depth of this chapter. For rare indeed in this age is one who can independently grasp this discourse, let alone master it and single-handedly carry its exposition to its conclusion. So we say:

The schools have diverged concerning co-extensiveness (al-ṭard), co-exclusiveness (al-ʿaks), and resemblance (al-shabah). Among them are those who affirmed one of the two (ṭard and ʿaks) without the other; among them are those who denied both; and among them are those who affirmed both. And we say: The school of al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah, and Mālik — may Allah have mercy on them — is the affirmation of both, for they affirmed resemblance (al-shabah), which is weaker than affirming co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness.

We shall first mention the proof, then proceed to the examples; and by the exposition of the examples, the proof becomes evident. For the proof of these examples is that we demonstrate that they yield preponderant conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann), and that is attained by striking an example.

As for the synoptic proof, it is what we have already mentioned concerning co-extensiveness and co-exclusiveness, namely: its summary. For we have established that the attribute — which differentiates between two states of a single essence — necessitates the attribution of the divergence in the ruling to it, because this is an actual divergence that did not previously exist; thus it requires a distinguishing mark (ʿalāmah) for its recognition, and that is none other than the apparent attribute. The foundation of this discourse is that no other newly-arisen attribute appears besides what was mentioned, and its appearance is possible. It is incumbent upon the mujtahid to search for it, and upon the one who provides the legal rationale (al-muʿallil) to rise to refute it when it is mentioned — and nothing is incumbent upon him before it is mentioned.

Likewise, the differentiator between two essences is like the differentiator between two states of a single essence.

Thus, when the Lawgiver says: "The killer does not inherit," we understand that killing is a mark of deprivation (ḥirmān), whether it is suitable (munāsib) or not. For had He said: "The tall one does not inherit," or "The black one does not inherit," we would say: Tallness and blackness are marks, and they entail an aspect of benefit (maṣlaḥah) that we do not perceive. And if this very wording had not been transmitted, but it were known from consensus (ijmāʿ) that he does not inherit — or the Prophet ﷺ had ruled concerning a person reported to have killed, that he does not inherit — we would still understand that killing is a mark of the difference between the heir and the non-heir, by virtue of its addition to another person who equals him in kinship. For it is said: He does not differ from him except in being a killer — so it (killing) is the operative basis (al-manāṭ) — just as it is said: The state of hardship does not differ from what preceded it except in hardship. Even if it is possible that the operative basis is a meaning entailed by killing, that does not prevent making killing a mark — unless it becomes evident that something entailed by it is more worthy of consideration than it.

The purpose is: That the attribution of a ruling to a person is like the attribution of a state to a state — in the judgment of the intellect regarding the impossibility of assigning the divergence to anything but the apparent differentiating attribute. And the completion of this consideration is by demonstrating that there is no differentiator besides it that rivals the apparent attribute, nor anything that the apparent attribute entails.

Likewise: If it is known that the black one does not inherit, then it is known that blackness is a mark — by contrasting him with the white one, just as it would be known by contrasting him with a prior state of that very same person in which he was white.

And likewise the case of slavery (al-riqq): It is known to be a mark of deprivation by positing its occurrence (ṭuryān) upon a single person, and by positing its addition to a free essence.

So the differentiator is sought between two essences, just as it is sought between two states. And when a differentiator is unavoidable — and there is no differentiator except the attribute claimed by the one providing the legal rationale — then it is the operative basis of the difference (manāṭ al-farq), provided it is conceded that there is no differentiator except that, as we have established in the case of the differentiator between two successive states upon a single essence. This runs — with respect to the mujtahid and the disputant providing the legal rationale — upon that very same course, for it is identical, and its proof is its proof. The aspect of the indication (wajh al-dalālah) is only clarified by striking examples.

In sum: It is not permissible to arbitrarily posit an attribute as a cause (ʿillah) by mere caprice. Rather —
