chapters.arabic_text:
### || CHECK الوجه الثاني: لامتناع الحكم مع وجود العلة

ملتفت إلى العادات؛ وعلى منهاجه يجري نظر الفقهاء، وهو عن منهاج الكلام
أبعد، ولذلك قيل: إن القائل بالخصوص في العلل فقيه محض، لأنه يجرد نظره إلى
العادات والمعتقدات الظاهرة. فنقول للذي سماه علة: ما الذي عنيت به؟ إن
عنيت وجوب الحكم بمجرده -وهذا حد العلة عندك -فهذا بمجرده لا يوجب الحكم،
دون نوع من الإضافة. وإن عنيت به أن الحكم يعرف بمجرد معرفته، دون أن تخطر
بالبال الإضافة -فهذا على هذا التأويل مسلم. وإذا كان اسم العلة مستعارا في
هذا المقام، فطريق الاستعارة متسعة، ولا حجر فيها بعد الإحاطة بالمقصود
المتعلق بالقضايا الاجتهادية، والجدلية، كما قررناها.
وتبين أن منشأ هذا الخصام العظيم: أنهم لم يتفقوا على حد واحد للعلة
معلوم؛ ولو وقع الاتفاق عليه: لهان عرض الوصف -المذكور في محل النزاع -على
ذلك [المحك]. فهذا كله في العلة القطعية.
ونحن نتعرض للوجوه الأخر في امتناع أحكام [العلل، قبل أن نتعرض لخصوص
العلة المستنبطة -: لنستوفي أولا الكلام] في وجوه الإضافات العقلية
واللفظية؛ إذ النظر في العلة المظنونة له مأخذ آخر.
الوجه الآخر لامتناع الحكم: أن يندفع بعد كمال العلة، بمعارضة علة دافعة،
كرق ولد المغرور: فغنه جرى فيه علة كاملة، وهو: ملك الأصل؛ غذ لا سبب لملك
أولاد الحيوانات إلا ملك الأصل. ولكن عارضه PageV01P486 # علة الحرية: اقترنت به، فدفعت حكمه. ولو لم يكن ذلك اندفاعا: لم وجب
الغرم: لأن الغرم لا يجب إلا بتفويت؛ ولا تفويت: إذ لا مفوت، ولكن: قيل:
دفعه في معنى قطعه. ولو اختل سبب الرق وانعدم، لكان انعدامه لا يوجب
الضمان؛ فإنه لو اعتق نصيبه من الجارية المشتركة، فأتت بولد -لم يغرم قيمة
الولد: لأنه انعقد على الحرية لانعدام سبب الرق. ولا غرم على معدم سبب الرق
في الولد: لأجل الوالد.
وكذلك: إذا زوج أمته من عبده، فاستحقاق البضع، علة استحقاق المهر. حتى
نقول: [لا ينفك عنه مع التفويض، ولا مهر في هذه الصورة، ولكن نقول:] سقط
بالرق  المقارن، فكان في حكم الواجب [الساقط] لا في حكم المنتفى من أصله
لانعدام سببه: لأن ملك السيد على العبد لو طرأ: [68 - ب] لبرأ ذمته من غير
أن يطرق خللا إلى سبب الاستحقاق؛ فإذا قارن دفع: وكان كما لو طرأ وقطع؛
فالمندفع في حكم المنقطع.
وكذلك القصاص الواجب: إذا انتقل بحكم الإرث إلى ابن من عليه القصاص -سقط.
ولو كان سبب استحقاق ابن القاتل مقترنا، لم يجب القصاص؛ وكان في معنى
الواجب الساقط. وقد عبر بعض أصحابنا عنه:
PageV01P487
بأنه وجب ثم سقط. فقيل له: إن سقط فلم وجب؟ وإن وجب مع الأبوة واقترانها،
فلم سقط؟ فكانت هذه اللفظة مختلة. والمعنى أنه في حكم الواجب الساقط: إذ
الحكم ثابت تقديرا. ولذلك قال بعض المحققين: من اشترى قريبه لم يدخل في
ملكه؛ بل عتق عليه واندفع ملكه. فاندفاع ملكه له حكم العتاق: إذ لو ملكه
لدام ملكه، والقرابة توجب نفي الملك: فتوجب دفع الملك، وهو دفع في معنى القطع.
وهذا استبعده فريق، وهو عندي سديد على هذا التأويل.
وكذلك قال الفقهاء: من نصب شبكة في مدارج الصيد، فتعاق به صيد بعد موته
-حصل الملك لورثته بطريق التلقي من المورث: حتى تقضي منه ديونه، وتنفذ فيه
وصاياه. ومعناه: أن علة ملك المورث جرت بكمالها؛ ولكن الموت دافع له فلتقاه
الوارث؛ فكان ذلك في معنى PageV01P488 # الانتقال تقديرا: لأنه بطريق التلقي منه، وإن كان الملك لا يصادف الميت
بحال. فالتلقي [منه] كالانتقال.
وكذلك قال بعض الفقهاء: الجناية في حق الجاني -في شبه العمد والخطأ -سبب
للوجوب؛ والعاقلة يتعرضون له بطريق التحمل، ولكن يجرى ذلك على وجه مختطف لا
يحس؛ ولكن يعقل تقديرا.
وقال أبو حنيفة -رضي الله عنه -: عقد الوكيل سبب في [وجوب حق الموكل]،
والملك يحصل للموكل بطريق التلقي منه على تقدير مختطف لا يدركه الحس، فيكون
في معنى الانتقال. حتى جوز لوكيل المسلم أن يشتري الخمر -إذا كان الوكيل
ذميا -بهذا الطريق.
فهذا متفق عليه بين العقلاء والفقهاء، وهو معقول كما تقرر، وهو:  [أن ما]
إذا طرأ قطع الحكم لا بتبعيض العلة، فإذا أقترن دفع، وكان PageV01P489 # الدفع في معنى القطع.
والغرض في هذا المقام أن نبين أن الحكم وإن اندفع، فالموجب علة محققة من
حيث اللفظ، والعقل، والاجتهاد، والجدل. ولا حاجة إلى الاحتراز عن مواضع
انتفاء الحكم، بهذا الطريق.
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Repelling, warding off, pushing back; the act of averting something that has reached its point of efficacy.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, the "repelling cause" (ʿillah dāfiʿah) is that which nullifies the effect of a complete cause without negating its causal status in itself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes physical repulsion; here it is metaphorical (majāz) for the juridical suspension of a ruling's efficacy.
- Root: ق-ط-ع (q-ṭ-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cutting, severing, interrupting; a decisive break in continuity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, "cutting off" (qaṭʿ) implies the total annihilation of the causal nexus, whereas "repelling" (dafʿ) implies a suspension that is functionally equivalent to cutting.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The phrase "repulsion is in the meaning of cutting" (al-dafʿ fī maʿnā al-qaṭʿ) is a recognized metaphorical extension, not a literal identity.
- Root: ت-ل-ق-ي (t-l-q-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Receiving, taking from another; the act of acquisition by transmission.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In inheritance law, the heir "receives" (talqqā) the right from the decedent, which is a notional (taqdīrī) transfer, not a physical one.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used metaphorically to equate "reception" with "transfer" (intiqāl) in legal fictions.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Taqdīr (Ellipsis and Notional Completion) — When a legal predicate is suspended, the grammar of the sentence requires positing an underlying notional state (e.g., "in the status of an obligation that has lapsed") to preserve syntactic and semantic coherence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second aspect — concerning the impossibility of the ruling [obtaining] despite the existence of the cause — is tied to customary practices; and upon this path the jurists' inquiry proceeds, and it is further removed from the path of theology (kalām). For this reason it was said: "He who affirms particularization (khuṣūṣ) in causes is a pure jurist," because he confines his inquiry to customs and apparent beliefs. So we say to the one who has named it a "cause": What did you intend by it? If you intended the necessitation of the ruling by its mere essence — and this is your definition of the cause — then this, by itself, does not necessitate the ruling, without some kind of relation (iḍāfah). But if you intended that the ruling is known by merely knowing it, without the relation occurring to the mind — then this, on this interpretation, is conceded. And since the name "cause" is borrowed (mustaʿār) in this context, the path of metaphorical borrowing is wide, and there is no restriction in it once the intended meaning concerning ijtihādī and dialectical (jadalī) matters is grasped, as we have established.

And it becomes clear that the source of this great dispute is that they did not agree upon a single, known definition of the cause; and had they agreed upon it, the examination of the attribute mentioned in the locus of dispute against that touchstone would have been easy. So all of this concerns the definitive cause (al-ʿillah al-qaṭʿiyyah).

And we now turn to the other aspects concerning the impossibility of the rulings of causes, before we address the particularization of the inferred cause (al-ʿillah al-mustanbaṭah) — so that we may first exhaust the discussion on the aspects of intellectual and verbal relations; for the inquiry into the probable cause has another avenue.

The other aspect for the impossibility of the ruling: that it is repelled after the completion of the cause, by the opposition of a repelling cause — like the slavery of the child of the deceived purchaser (al-magh rūr): for a complete cause ran in it, namely, the ownership of the origin (milk al-aṣl); for there is no cause for the ownership of the offspring of animals except the ownership of the origin. But it was opposed by the cause of freedom (al-ḥurriyyah): it was conjoined with it, and repelled its ruling. And had this not been a repulsion, why then would indemnity (ghurm) be obligatory? For indemnity is not obligatory except for destruction (tafwīt); and there is no destruction, since there is no destroyer. But it was said: "Its repulsion is in the meaning of its cutting off." And had the cause of slavery been vitiated and become non-existent, its non-existence would not necessitate liability; for if a man freed his share of a jointly-owned slave-girl, and she then gave birth — he would not owe the value of the child: because it was conceived upon freedom due to the non-existence of the cause of slavery. And no liability falls upon the one who annihilates the cause of slavery in the offspring, on account of the parent.

Likewise: when a man marries his female slave to his male slave, the entitlement to sexual access (istiḥqāq al-baḍʿ) is the cause of the entitlement to the dowry (mahr). Until we say: "It is not separable from it with delegation (tafwīḍ), and there is no dowry in this case — but we say: It fell due to the conjoined slavery, so it was in the status of an obligation that has lapsed (al-wājib al-sāqiṭ), not in the status of one negated from its origin due to the non-existence of its cause." For had the master's ownership of the slave supervened [after the contract], it would have discharged his liability without introducing any defect into the cause of entitlement; so when it is conjoined, it repels, and it is as though it supervened and cut off; so the repelled is in the status of the cut off.

Likewise, the obligatory retaliation (qiṣāṣ): when it is transferred by the rule of inheritance to a son of the one upon whom retaliation is due — it lapses. And had the cause of the killer's son's entitlement been conjoined, retaliation would not be obligatory; and it would be in the meaning of an obligation that has lapsed. And some of our companions expressed it thus: "It was obligatory, then it lapsed." So it was said to him: "If it lapsed, then why was it obligatory? And if it was obligatory with the paternity and its conjunction, then why did it lapse?" So this expression was defective. And the meaning is that it is in the status of an obligation that has lapsed: for the ruling is established notionally (taqdīran). For this reason, some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) said: "Whoever purchases his relative, he does not enter into his ownership; rather, he is freed upon him, and his ownership is repelled." So the repulsion of his ownership has the ruling of emancipation: for had he owned him, his ownership would have persisted, and kinship necessitates the negation of ownership; so it necessitates the repulsion of ownership, and it is a repulsion in the meaning of cutting. And a group deemed this far-fetched, but in my view it is sound upon this interpretation.

Likewise, the jurists said: "Whoever sets a net in the paths of game, and game becomes entangled in it after his death — ownership accrues to his heirs by way of reception (talqqī) from the decedent: so that his debts are settled from it, and his bequests are executed from it." And its meaning is: the cause of the decedent's ownership ran to its completion; but death repelled it, so the heir received it; so that was in the meaning of transfer, notionally: because it is by way of reception from him, even though ownership does not encounter the deceased in any state. So reception from him is like transfer.

Likewise, some jurists said: "The offense (jināyah) in the case of the offender — in quasi-intentional (shibh al-ʿamd) and erroneous (khaṭaʾ) [homicide] — is a cause for obligation; and the ʿāqilah (the kin-group liable for blood-money) are exposed to it by way of bearing (taḥammul), but this runs in a subtle manner (wajh mukhtataf) that is not perceived [by sense]; yet it is understood notionally."

And Abū Ḥanīfah — may God be pleased with him — said: "The contract of the agent (wakīl) is a cause for the obligation of the principal's right, and ownership accrues to the principal by way of reception from him upon a subtle estimation not grasped by sense, so it is in the meaning of transfer." To the extent that he permitted the agent of a Muslim to purchase wine — if the agent were a dhimmī — by this path.

So this is agreed upon among the rational people and the jurists, and it is intelligible as established, namely: that what, when it supervenes, cuts off the ruling without partitioning the cause — when it is conjoined, it repels, and the repulsion is in the meaning of cutting.

And the purpose in this context is to show that the ruling, even if repelled, the obligating factor is a verified cause (ʿillah muḥaqqiqah) from the perspectives of language, reason, ijtihād, and dialectic. And there is no need to guard against the loci where the ruling is negated by this path.

chapters.title_en: The Third Aspect: The Non-Realization of the Ruling Despite the Existence of the Cause — Due to a Defect in the Locus, the Agent, or the Condition
chapters.arabic_text:
### || AUTO الوجه الثالث: لانتفاء الحكم مع وجود العلة

: أن ينتفي لا لخلل في ركن العلة، ولكن لخلل في المحل والأهل والشرط،
كقولنا: أن البيع سبب لزوال الملك وعلة له. وللبيع ركن، وهو: صيغة الإيجاب
والقبول. وله مصدر، وهو: العاقد. وشرطه: [أن يكون عاقلا بالغا مالكا. وله
موقع ومنزل، وهو: المبيع، وشرطه]: أن يكون مالا متقوما مقدورا على تسليمه.
إلى غير ذلك من الشرائط. والفقهاء يطلقون القول بأن البيع هو السبب والعلة،
مع علمهم بأن الحكم لا يتعلق بمجرد وجود صيغة البيع، ما لم تصدر عن مصدر
مخصوص، ولم تضف إلى محل مخصوص.
فنقدم في هذا الطرف القضية العقلية واللفظية، فنقول: لا وجه لتسميته علة
على مذهب من يأخذ العلة من مثال العلل العقلية؛ فإن الموجب للحكم بيع مضاف
إلى عاقد مخصوص مصادف لمعقود مخصوص، فالعلة عبارة عن البيع الموصوف بسائر
الأوصاف. فإذا لم يحصل الملك: كان PageV01P490 # ذلك لانعدام العلة والسبب. وإليه يشير مسلك الأستاذ، فيقول: لا فرق بين
أن يمتنع الحكم لفقد الإيجاب والقبول أو لخلل فيه، وبين أن يمتنع لصدوره من
الصبي، وبين أن يمتنع لمصادفته خمرا. فالكل ممتنع لامتناع السبب. فإذا باع
الصبي، بطل: لعدم السبب. وإذا بيع الخمر، بطل: لعدم السبب. وإذا بيع واختل
الإيجاب والقبول، بطل: لعدم السبب. فإن السبب المشروع -الذي هو علة لإفادة
الحكم -: بيع مضاف إلى عاقد مخصوص، وإلى معقود مخصوص. ففقد بعض الأوصاف فقد
لسبب والعلة.
فعلى هذا، إذا قال الحنفي مثلا: الغصب سبب لملك بدل المغصوب، فكان سببا
لملك المغصوب أو كان علة له -ينتقض بالغصب في المدبر. وقد اختلف الجدليون
في ذلك، فمنهم من قال: هذا النقض غير لازم؛ فإنا نقول: الغصب في المدبر
سبب، ولكن المحل غير قابل للتمليك، ولذلك لا يقبل البيع. ومن الجدليين من
زاد احترازا وقال: فينبغي أن يفيد الملك في المحل القابل [للتمليك].
وكذلك إذا قلنا: ملك الصبي كامل: فكان سببا لوجوب الزكاة؛ PageV01P491 # فقيل لنا: باطل بملكه فيما دون النصاب. إلى أمثال له، فهو النقض المائل
عن مقصد التعليل، الوارد على صورة اللفظ. ونحن نقول: القضية الاجتهادية في
هذا الجنس معلومة؛ إذ لا يجوز للمجتهد أن يفتي بحصول الملك بمجرد ملاحظة
البيع، ما لم يلحظ اتصافه بقيوده، وإضافاته.
فإنما الموجب للحكم بيع موصوف بالإضافة إلى شخص مخصوص ومحل مخصوص. فإذا
صادف جميع القيود والإضافات [حاصلة]: حكم بالملك وإلا فلا.
وأما القضية الجدلية، فالذي نراه فيها أن هذا النقض غير لازم: لأنه مائل
عن مقصد الكلام. فإنا وإن كنا نعلم أن موجب الحكم مركب من جملة الأوصاف،
ولكن جهات النظر ونواحيها متباعدة. فليس بطلان بيع الصبي من جهة بطلان بيع
الخمر. بل يقال: لا خلل في الركن وهو: الإيجاب والقبول. وإنما الخلل في صفة
العاقد. فيطلب مأخذه؛ ومأخذه يبعد [69 - أ] عن مأخذ صفات المعقود وصيغة
الإيجاب والقبول. فنقول: بيعه سبب صادف محله ولكن لم يصدر من أهله، وبيع
الخمر صدر من أهله ولكن لم يصادف محله؛ فتتباعد مقاصد النظر، وتتباين
مآخذه.
PageV01P492
فإذا كان المقصود البحث عن جهة، فتعرض المعلل لمأخذها -فلا ينبغي أن
يناقض بما ينشأ النظر فيه من ناحية أخرى بعيدة عن مقصد النظر.
فإذا قال القائل: الصبي أهل للبيع، لم يحسن أن يقال: لو كان أهلا لصح منه
بيع الخمر.
وإذا قال: المبيع [الغائب] محل للبيع، لم يحسن أن يقال: لو كان كذلك لصح
[فيه] بيع الصبي، فإنه وإن بطل بيع الصبي فيه، لم يناقض قوله: هو محل
البيع. وكان مثاله من كلام الشارع صلوات الله عليه قوله: "في سائمة الغنم
الزكاة" وما دون النصاب سائمة، ولا زكاة فيه. ولا يعد نقضا لهذا الكلام:
لأنه منحرف عن مقصود الكلام.
وقد قال عز وجل: "والسارق والسارقة فاقطعوا أيديهما  جزاء بما كسبا" فجعل
السرقة علة للقطع؛ وسرقة ما دون النصاب سرقة PageV01P493 # وليس بعلة، ولا يعد ذلك نقضا ولا مناقضا؛ لأن مقصود الكلام التعرض للجهة
والسبب، لا للمحل الذي يعمل فيه السبب.
فهذا ما نراه في القضية الجدلية، وهو: رد كل نقض منحرف عن مقصد الكلام؛
كما ذكرناه.
وكذلك لا نرى انتقاض قول الحنفي بالمدبر، إذ قال: الغصب سبب ملك البدل،
فليكن سبب ملك الأصل، لأنه يقول: هو في المدبر -أيضا -سبب؛ فليس من مقصوده
التعرض للمحل الذي يعمل فيه السبب. وهذا عبر الجدليون عنه: بأن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes a recurring state or attribute that necessitates an effect; a "cause" (ʿillah) is that which entails its consequent by virtue of its very description.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juridical theology (uṣūl al-fiqh), the ʿillah is the effective attribute (waṣf) upon which the ruling (ḥukm) is predicated — not the mere existence of an act, but its qualified instantiation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The term is used metaphorically (majāz) when extended from rational causes to legal causes; the literal sense (ḥaqīqah) requires the full conjunction of all qualifying attributes.
- Root: س-ب-ب (s-b-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A "rope" or "cord" that connects one thing to another; hence, a means or pathway (ṭarīq) leading to an effect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, the sabab is the manifest occasion (amārah) that the Lawgiver has made the sign for the ruling, distinct from the ʿillah in that it may subsist without the full conditions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally a physical connector; metaphorically, the legal instrument (e.g., sale) that links the agent and the object to the transfer of ownership.
- Root: م-ح-ل (m-ḥ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The "place" or "locus" where something settles and becomes operative.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The substrate (maḥall) that must be receptive (qābil) for the ruling to attach; if the substrate is non-receptive, the cause is present but the effect is absent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal spatial location; metaphorical extension to the legal subject-matter (e.g., the sold item) that must possess the requisite attributes.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-Ḥukm ʿalā al-Ṣifah al-Majmūʿah (Attribution of the Ruling to the Composite Description) — The predicate (ḥukm) is grammatically and logically attached to the entire qualified noun phrase (al-mawṣūf bi-ṣifātihi), not to the bare noun; thus, any missing qualifier negates the predicate, just as a sentence is incomplete without all its syntactic complements.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third aspect [of the invalidation of a cause] is that the ruling is absent not due to a defect in the pillar (rukn) of the cause, but rather due to a defect in the locus (maḥall), the agent (ahl), or the condition (sharṭ).

For example, our statement: "Sale (al-bayʿ) is a cause (sabab) for the transfer of ownership and an effective cause (ʿillah) for it." Sale has a pillar, namely: the formula of offer and acceptance (ṣīghat al-ījāb wa al-qabūl). It has a source (maṣdar), namely: the contracting party (al-ʿāqid). Its condition is that he be sane, of age, and possess legal capacity. It has a locus and station (mawqiʿ wa manzil), namely: the sold item (al-mabīʿ), and its condition is that it be valuable property (mālan mutaqawwiman), capable of being delivered. And there are other conditions besides these. Yet the jurists (fuqahāʾ) freely state that sale is the cause (sabab) and the effective cause (ʿillah), while knowing full well that the ruling does not attach to the mere existence of the sale formula, unless it issues from a specific source and is added to a specific locus.

So we advance in this regard the rational and linguistic proposition, and we say: There is no justification for calling it a "cause" (ʿillah) according to the school that derives the cause from the model of rational causes. For that which necessitates the ruling is a sale that is qualified by its addition to a specific contracting party and its coincidence with a specific object of contract. Thus, the cause is the sale described by all its attributes (al-bayʿ al-mawṣūf bi-sāʾir al-awṣāf). So when ownership is not realized, that is due to the non-existence of the cause and the means (sabab). And to this the method of the Master (al-Ustādh) alludes, for he says: There is no difference between the ruling being prevented by the absence of offer and acceptance or by a defect therein, and its being prevented by its issuance from a minor, and its being prevented by its coinciding with wine. For all of these are prevented due to the prevention of the cause (imtināʿ al-sabab). So when a minor sells, the sale is void: due to the non-existence of the cause. When wine is sold, it is void: due to the non-existence of the cause. When a sale occurs but the offer and acceptance are defective, it is void: due to the non-existence of the cause. For the legislated cause — which is the effective cause for producing the ruling — is a sale added to a specific contracting party and to a specific object of contract. So the loss of any of its attributes is the loss of the cause and the effective cause.

On this basis, if a Ḥanafī, for example, says: "Usurpation (al-ghaṣb) is a cause for ownership of the substitute for the usurped property," and thus it would be a cause for ownership of the usurped property itself or an effective cause for it — this is invalidated (yuntaqaḍ) by usurpation in the case of a mudabbar (a slave whose emancipation is deferred upon the master's death). The dialecticians (jadaliyyūn) have differed regarding this. Among them are those who say: This invalidation (naqḍ) is not binding; for we say: Usurpation in the case of the mudabbar is a cause, but the locus is not receptive to being owned (ghayr qābil lil-tamlīk), and therefore it does not accept sale. And among the dialecticians are those who added a precautionary qualification (iḥtirāz) and said: It should rather produce ownership in a locus that is receptive to being owned.

Likewise, if we say: "The ownership of a minor is complete (kāmil), and thus it is a cause for the obligation of zakāh," and it is said to us: "This is invalidated by his ownership of less than the niṣāb (the threshold amount)," and similar examples — this is the invalidation that deviates from the purpose of the causal explanation (al-naqḍ al-māʾil ʿan maqṣad al-taʿlīl), which is directed at the form of the wording. And we say: The ijtihādī proposition in this genre is known; for it is not permissible for a mujtahid to issue a legal opinion (fatwā) that ownership is realized merely by observing the sale, unless he observes its being qualified by its restrictions (quyūd) and its additions (iḍāfāt).

For that which necessitates the ruling is a sale described by its addition to a specific person and a specific locus. So if it coincides with all the restrictions and additions being present, he rules for ownership; otherwise, not.

As for the dialectical proposition (al-qaḍiyyah al-jadaliyyah), what we hold regarding it is that this invalidation is not binding: because it deviates from the purpose of the discourse (maqṣad al-kalām). For even though we know that that which necessitates the ruling is composed of a totality of attributes, nevertheless the aspects of consideration (jihāt al-naẓar) and their directions are far apart. For the nullity of a minor's sale is not from the same direction as the nullity of the sale of wine. Rather, it is said: There is no defect in the pillar, namely: the offer and acceptance. The defect is only in the attribute of the contracting party. So one seeks its source (maʾkhadh); and its source is far from the source of the attributes of the object of contract and the formula of offer and acceptance. So we say: His sale is a cause that coincided with its locus but did not issue from its proper agent; and the sale of wine issued from its proper agent but did not coincide with its locus. Thus the purposes of consideration diverge, and their sources become distinct.

So when the purpose is to investigate a particular aspect (jihah), and the one who provides the causal explanation (al-muʿallil) addresses its source — then it is not fitting that he be invalidated by what arises in consideration from another direction far from the purpose of the investigation.

So if someone says: "The minor is qualified (ahl) for sale," it is not proper to say: "If he were qualified, then his sale of wine would be valid."

And if someone says: "The absent item (al-mabīʿ al-ghāʾib) is a locus for sale," it is not proper to say: "If that were so, then the minor's sale would be valid in it." For even though the minor's sale in it is void, that does not contradict his statement: "It is a locus for sale." And an example of this from the speech of the Lawgiver — peace and blessings be upon him — is his saying: {«فِي سَائِمَةِ الْغَنَمِ الزَّكَاةُ»} ("In freely grazing sheep, there is zakāh") — and what is less than the niṣāb is freely grazing, yet there is no zakāh in it. And this is not counted as an invalidation of this statement: because it deviates from the purpose of the discourse.

And Allah — Glorified and Exalted — has said: {«وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ فَاقْطَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمَا جَزَاءً بِمَا كَسَبَا»} ("And the male thief and the female thief: cut off their hands as recompense for what they have earned") — so He made theft a cause for amputation; and the theft of less than the niṣāb is theft, yet it is not a cause, and this is not counted as an invalidation nor a contradiction; because the purpose of the discourse is to address the aspect and the cause, not the locus in which the cause operates.

This, then, is what we hold regarding the dialectical proposition, namely: the rejection of every invalidation that deviates from the purpose of the discourse, as we have mentioned.

Likewise, we do not hold that the Ḥanafī's statement is invalidated by the case of the mudabbar, when he says: "Usurpation is a cause for ownership of the substitute, so let it be a cause for ownership of the original" — because he says: "It is, in the case of the mudabbar, also a cause." So it is not his purpose to address the locus in which the cause operates. And this is what the dialecticians have expressed by saying: [that the invalidation is rejected when it deviates from the intended aspect of the causal explanation].

chapters.title_en: The Attribute Qualifying the Sentence is Not Contradicted by Detailed Specification
chapters.arabic_text:
### || AUTO المعلل للجملة لا يناقض بالتفصيل

. فهذا ما يتعلق بالقضية الجدلية، والاجتهادية.
أما القضية [العقلية والاسمية]، فنقول فيها: تسمية السرقة المطلقة علة في
القطع لا يستقيم على مذهب من يأخذ حد العلة من العقلية؛ لأن العلة الموجبة
سرقة مضافة مخصوصة، فلا يضاف الحكم عقلا إلى السرقة المطلقة، ولا تسمى
السرقة المطلقة عن قيد الإضافة علة، فالعلة سرقة مقيدة بجميع قيودها. وكذلك
البيع والقتل والزنا، وجميع الأسباب، فلا يسمى مطلقها علة. أما من يأخذ اسم
العلة من ظهور الحكم بسبب حدوثه، فالحادث المتجدد هو السرقة والقتل والبيع
[والزنا].
PageV01P494
فأما أوصاف الفاعل والمحل فسابق؛ فيضاف الحكم إلى الحوادث لا إلى أوصاف
المحل، وإن كان أوصاف المحال والفاعلين شروطا لحصول المقاصد، كما ضربناه:
من أمثال المردي في البئر؛ والعلة العارضة الموجبة للضعف. وهذا المسلك أقرب
إلى الفقه.
وقد فرق الفقهاء بين ما قبل وجود السبب، وبين ما بعده -في الأحكام؛
والوجوب منتف في الحالتين جميعا. فجوزوا تقديم الزكاة بعد وجود ملك النصاب
وقبل انقضاء الحول، ولم يجوزوا قبل ملك النصاب. وجوزوا تقديم الكفارة على
الحنث بعد وجود اليمين، ولم يجوزوا [قبل اليمين]؛ والوجوب منتف في
الحالتين: اعتمادا على سبب الوجوب. فسموه سببا وإن لم يتصل به الوجوب،
فتسميته علة على هذا التأويل -أيضا -غير بعيد.
وكذلك جوزوا التكفير عن القتل بعد الجرح، بالمال وبالصوم PageV01P495 # الذي هو عبادة لا تقدم على وقتها.
وتستمد هذه التسمية الفقهية المعتضدة بالعرفيات  التي قدمنا أمثلتها من
قضية في الإضافة عقلية؛ فإن الذات الموصوفة بصفات، إذا أوجبت حكما: أشارت
العقول إلى الإضافة إلى الذات دون الصفات، فإن الصفات توابع، فلا تجعل ركنا
مع الذات وجزءا من الموجب. فالكتابة إذا حدثت من جهة الكاتب: أضيفت إلى
الكاتب لا إلى العلم والقدرة والقصد والإرادة وإن كنا نعلم أن ذات الكاتب
لا تحدث الكتابة إلا بعد الاتصاف بهذه الصفات.
وكذلك: إحداث العالم مضاف إلى الإله -عز وجل -في ذاته، فيقال: هو المحدث؛
وتستقيم الإضافة إلى مجرد الذات، دون التعرض للصفات.
فإن قال قائل: هو إشارة إلى ذاته الموصوفة بصفاته، قلنا: يجوز أن يقال:
زيد محدث هذه الكتابة، فيضاف الإحداث إلى ذات زيد:
PageV01P496
وليس زيد عبارة عن الذات مع العلم والإرادة والقصد، فإنه -مع الانفكاك عن
هذه الصفات -تعقل ذاته، وزيد إشارة إليه لا إلى الصفات.
فكذلك بهذه القضية العقلية، تستقيم إضافة حدوث الملك إلى البيع في ذاته،
وحدوث وجوب العقوبات إلى القتل والسرقة والزنا في ذواتها.
فإن قولنا: بيع مكلف"، [إضافة؛ وهو:] صفة البيع لا يعقل قيامه إلا
بالبيع. وقولنا: سرقة نصاب"، إضافة إلى السرقة. والإضافة صفة تابعة للمضاف
إليه، فكان الذات في نفسها هي التي يضاف إليها، دون الأوصاف التابعة. وبهذا
تنفصل عن أجزاء العلة وأبعاض أركانها: إذ ليس بعضها، تابعا للبعض، فهو
كالإيجاب والقبول: لا يضاف الحكم إلى واحد، بل يضاف إليهما. فالسبب يتركب
منهما، وليس أحدهما وصفا للآخر.
ولذلك، قلنا: لو ملك نصف النصاب وعجل نصف شاة: لم يجز، ولو ملك كمال
النصاب وعجل الزكاة قبل انقضاء الحول: جاز. لأن الموجب هو نصاب باق حولا؛
وكونه باقيا صفة النصاب: فلم يكن ركن العلة وبعض السبب. فجاز التقديم بعد
وجود أصل
PageV01P497
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Recurrence of an event; the secondary cause or occasion (ʿillah) that necessitates a ruling; also, the defect or infirmity that alters a state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory (uṣūl al-fiqh), the ʿillah is the effective cause that grounds a ruling (ḥukm), distinguished from mere condition (sharṭ) or sign (amārah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes the cause that brings about an effect; metaphorical extension applies to legal attribution where the cause is inferred from the observable occasioning event.
- Root: ض-ا-ف (ḍ-ā-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To incline, annex, or attribute; grammatical annexation (iḍāfah) where one noun is related to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Relational attribution of an act or ruling to its agent or occasion, distinguishing the essence (dhāt) from its attributes (ṣifāt).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal annexation in grammar; metaphorical in theology—attributing creation to God’s essence without explicit mention of His attributes.
- Root: س-ب-ب (s-b-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A rope or cord by which something is tied; hence, a means or cause connecting an act to its consequence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, the sabab is the occasioning ground for a ruling’s obligation (wujūb), even if the obligation is deferred or suspended.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a physical tie; metaphorical: the legal nexus between an event and its normative effect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-Iḍāfah al-Maʿnawiyyah (Semantic Annexation) — When a noun is annexed to another, the annexed noun (muḍāf) is qualified by the annexation, and the compound functions as a single conceptual unit; thus, attribution of an act to the essence (dhāt) excludes the dependent attributes (ṣifāt tābiʿah), which are not integral parts of the cause.
chapters.translation:
I say: This concludes what pertains to the dialectical and jurisprudential proposition.

As for the rational and nominal proposition, we state therein: The designation of absolute theft as a cause (ʿillah) for amputation is not sound upon the doctrine of one who derives the definition of cause from rational principles; for the necessitating cause is a specific, qualified theft, so the ruling is not rationally attributed to absolute theft, nor is theft stripped of the qualifier of annexation termed a cause. Rather, the cause is theft restricted by all its qualifications. Likewise with sale, homicide, and fornication—and all causes—their unqualified forms are not termed causes. As for one who takes the name of cause from the manifestation of the ruling due to its occurrence, the newly occurring event is the theft, homicide, sale, or fornication.

As for the attributes of the agent and the locus, these are antecedent; thus the ruling is attributed to the occurring events, not to the attributes of the locus—even if the attributes of the loci and agents are conditions for the attainment of the objectives, as we exemplified with the case of the one who falls into a well, and the incidental cause necessitating weakness. This path is closer to jurisprudence.

The jurists have distinguished between what precedes the existence of the cause and what follows it—in the rulings—while obligation (wujūb) is negated in both states alike. Thus they permitted the advancement of zakāh after the existence of ownership of the nisāb but before the completion of the year, and did not permit it before ownership of the nisāb. They permitted the advancement of the expiation (kaffārah) upon the oath before the violation (ḥanath) after the existence of the oath, and did not permit it before the oath—while obligation is negated in both states—relying upon the cause of obligation. So they termed it a cause (sabab) even though obligation was not attached to it; thus terming it a cause (ʿillah) upon this interpretation is also not remote.

Likewise, they permitted expiation for homicide after the wounding, whether by wealth or by fasting—which is an act of worship not to be advanced before its time.

And this jurisprudential designation, supported by the customary usages we have previously exemplified, derives from a rational proposition concerning annexation; for when a substance described by attributes necessitates a ruling, the intellects point to annexation to the substance rather than to the attributes—for the attributes are dependent (tawābiʿ), so they are not made a pillar alongside the substance nor a part of the necessitating cause. Thus, when writing occurs from the direction of the writer, it is attributed to the writer, not to knowledge, power, intent, or will—even though we know that the writer’s substance does not produce writing except after being qualified by these attributes.

Likewise: The origination of the world is attributed to the Divine—mighty and majestic—in His essence, so it is said: He is the Originator; and the annexation is sound to the mere essence, without addressing the attributes.

If someone says: It is an indication of His essence qualified by His attributes, we reply: It is permissible to say, “Zayd originated this writing,” and the origination is attributed to Zayd’s essence—and Zayd is not an expression for the essence along with knowledge, will, and intent; for even with separation from these attributes, his essence is conceived, and “Zayd” indicates him, not the attributes.

Thus, by this rational proposition, the annexation of the occurrence of ownership to sale in its essence is sound, and the occurrence of the obligation of punishments to homicide, theft, and fornication in their essences.

For our saying “a sale by a legally responsible person” is an annexation—it is an attribute of the sale that is not conceived to subsist except through the sale. And our saying “theft of a nisāb” is an annexation to the theft. The annexation is an attribute dependent upon the annexed-to (muḍāf ilayh); so the substance in itself is that to which annexation is made, not the dependent attributes. And by this, it is distinguished from the parts of the cause and the limbs of its pillars: for they are not such that one is dependent upon another—like offer and acceptance: the ruling is not attributed to one alone, but to both together. For the cause is composed of them, and neither is an attribute of the other.

For this reason, we said: If one owned half the nisāb and advanced half a sheep, it is not permissible; but if one owned the complete nisāb and advanced the zakāh before the completion of the year, it is permissible. For the necessitating cause is a nisāb remaining for a full year; and its remaining is an attribute of the nisāb—so it is not a pillar of the cause nor a part of the sabab. Thus advancement is permissible after the existence of the origin.

chapters.title_en: The Condition, the Pillar, and the Locus — Clarifying Their Distinction from the Cause
chapters.arabic_text:
### || CHECK الشرط والركن والمحل

السبب. ونصف النصاب بعض السبب وأحد أركانه؛ فلم يمكن أن يجعل تابعا وتقدم
بسبب وجوده الزكاة.
فهذه قضايا عقلية: تتأيد بالعادات، وتؤيد المصير إلى تسمية الأسباب
[عللا]، وإضافة الأحكام إليها إذا حدثت، وإن كان الحكم لا يجب بمطلقها
وبمجردها؛  وإنما يجب بموصوفها بإضافات. ولكن الحكم يضاف -عقلا [69 - ب]
وعرفا ولغة -إلى الذات الموصوفة؛ فجاز تسميتها علة بهذا الطريق. وبان أن
ذلك جار في الجدل على الوجه الذي قررناه، ونبهنا على القضية الاجتهادية فيه أيضا.
فإن قال قائل: سياق كلامكم يدل على أن العاقد والمبيع في مقام الشرط
والمحل في البيع، وليس في مقام الركن. ونحن نعلم أن البيع لا ينعقد بيعا
دون مبيع، فالمبيع هو الركن، فكيف يقال: أنه محل يجري مجرى الشرط؟
قلنا: الشرط والمحل والركن عبارات أطلقها الفقهاء، وغمض مدركها على
الأكثر؛ لأنهم يعبرون بها عن مقاصد مختلفة، ولم يتفقوا فيها على حد معلوم
بالاصطلاح. ونحن ننبه على الغرض، ثم لا حرج في الاطلاقات، فنقول: القتل لا
يتصور إلا بقاتل وقتيل وفعل يسمى قتلا؛ وإذا وجب القصاص فإنما يجب بالقتل.
ولا يتصور [أن ينفعل القتل قتلا] إلا بالقتيل والقاتل، [وفعل يسمى قتلا].
ولكن لا تجعل PageV01P498 # حياة القتيل ووجوده بعضا من موجب القصاص ولا ركنا، ولكن يحال الحكم على
القتل المجرد، ثم نعلم أن القتل لا ينفعل قتلا إلا بحياة المقتول ووجوده
ووجود الفاعل، ولكن القصاص يضاف إلى ما يضاف إليه الهلاك، والهلاك يضاف إلى
الفعل وهو: الجرح، لا إلى محل الجرح وفاعل الجرح؛ وإن كان الجرح لا ينفعل
جرحا إلا بفاعل ومحل.
فهذه أمور معقولة ينبغي أن تتحقق أولا، ثم إذا تحققت: اصطلح الفقهاء على
التعبير عما يضاف إليه [الحكم]: بالسبب والعلة؛ وعلى التعبير عما لا ينفعل
السبب إلا بوجوده: بالشرط والمحل.
ثم ركن السبب عبارة عن نفس السبب وذاته، فإن اتحد ذاته: اتحد الركن؛ وإن
تعدد ذاته كالإيجاب والقبول: سمي أحد العددين ركنا من أركان العلة وبعضا من
أبعاضها، ولم تسم الشروط ركنا وبعضا من ذات السبب.
فهذه اصطلاحات الفقهاء بينة، ومقاصدها معلومة، ولا حجر -بعد الإحاطة بها
-في المضايقة فيها، والمساهلة عليها. هذا: مع العلم بأن الحكم ينتفي عند
انتفاء الشرط والمحل، كما ينتفي عند انتفاء السبب. فلا رجم عند عدم الزنا،
ولا رجم  -أيضا -عند عدم الإحصان، ولكن جهات الانتفاء هي المختلفة. ولما
تباينت جهات النظر، وتعددت في PageV01P499 # أنفسها، واختلفت خواصها -اصطلح الفقهاء على عبارات متعددة: تنبئ
-باصطلاحهم -عن مقاصدها. فهذا فن الفقه. وهو اللائق به.
والقول المائل عنه، بتقدير جميع الأوصاف قيودا للعلة وأبعاضا وأركانا
لها: من حيث كان الوجود موقوفا على جميعها -مستمد من فن الكلام، كما نبهنا عليه.
ولن يتصور الخلاف في هذه المسئلة: من حيث المعنى؛ وإنما يرجع ذلك إلى
التسمية، أو إلى الإضافة المعلومة بالعادة؛ على ما ذكرناها.
هذا تمام البيان فيما يتعلق بامتناع الحكم [لعارض مدافع] هو في حكم
القاطع، وفي امتناعه لفقد شرط ومحل.
والآن ننعطف على المقصود الذي كنا فيه، وهو: بيان ورود

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-ر-ط (sharṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A mark, sign, or stipulation; that which is conditional and upon which something else depends for its existence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, a sharṭ is that whose absence entails the absence of the ruling, but whose presence does not necessitate the ruling's presence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes a binding condition; metaphorical extension applies to any prerequisite for actualization.
- Root: ر-ك-ن (rukn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The corner or pillar of a structure; that which constitutes the essential support.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intrinsic part of an act or entity without which the act or entity cannot be conceived as such.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for architectural support; metaphorical for the constitutive essence of a legal act.
- Root: م-ح-ل (maḥall)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The place or locus where something occurs or inheres.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The substrate in which an accident or act is realized; distinct from the agent and the act itself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial location; metaphorical for the subject receiving an effect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When terms like "condition," "pillar," and "locus" are juxtaposed, their syntactic coordination signals conceptual distinction yet functional interdependence, requiring precise parsing of each term's referent.
chapters.translation:
I say: The cause (al-sabab). Half of the nisāb (the minimum threshold for zakāh) is part of the cause and one of its pillars; thus it could not be made subordinate and prior, because the zakāh is necessitated by the existence of the cause.

These are rational matters (qaḍāyā ʿaqliyyah): they are reinforced by customary practice, and they support the recourse to naming causes "illal" (legal rationales) and attributing rulings to them when they occur — even though the ruling is not necessitated by the cause in its absolute and bare form, but only by the cause as qualified by its additional attributes. Nevertheless, the ruling is attributed — rationally, conventionally, and linguistically — to the qualified essence itself; so it is permissible to call it a "cause" (ʿillah) in this manner. And it has become clear that this applies in dialectical disputation (jadal) in the manner we have established, and we have also drawn attention to the ijtihādī aspect of this matter therein.

If someone says: "The drift of your discourse indicates that the contracting party and the object of sale stand in the position of the condition and the locus in the sale, not in the position of the pillar. Yet we know that a sale does not contract as a sale without an object of sale — so the object of sale is the pillar. How then can it be said that it is a locus that runs in the course of the condition?"

We reply: "Condition," "locus," and "pillar" are expressions employed by the jurists (fuqahāʾ), yet their precise referents have remained obscure to most, because they use them for different purposes, and they have not agreed upon a fixed technical definition. We shall now draw attention to the intended meaning, and then there is no restriction on the various usages. So we say: Homicide (al-qatl) is not conceivable except with a killer, a victim, and an act called "killing." When retaliation (qiṣāṣ) becomes obligatory, it is obligatory only by virtue of the killing. And the killing cannot be actualized as killing except through the victim, the killer, and an act called "killing." But the life of the victim and his existence are not made a part of the cause of retaliation, nor a pillar thereof; rather, the ruling is referred to the bare killing. Then we know that the killing is not actualized as killing except through the life of the slain, his existence, and the existence of the agent. However, retaliation is attributed to that to which the destruction is attributed, and the destruction is attributed to the act — namely, the wounding — not to the locus of the wounding nor to the agent of the wounding; even though the wounding is not actualized as wounding except through an agent and a locus.

These are intelligible matters that ought to be ascertained first. Once they are ascertained, the jurists have conventionally agreed to express that to which the ruling is attributed as "the cause" (al-sabab) and "the rationale" (al-ʿillah), and to express that without whose existence the cause is not actualized as "the condition" (al-sharṭ) and "the locus" (al-maḥall).

Then, the "pillar of the cause" (rukn al-sabab) is an expression for the very cause itself and its essence. If its essence is unitary, then the pillar is unitary; if its essence is multiple — as in the case of offer (ījāb) and acceptance (qabūl) — then one of the two is called a pillar of the cause and a part of its parts, while the conditions are not called a pillar nor a part of the cause's essence.

These are the jurists' conventions, which are clear, and their purposes are known. Once one has grasped them, there is no restriction in being either stringent or lenient in these terminologies. This is so, while knowing that the ruling is negated upon the negation of the condition and the locus, just as it is negated upon the negation of the cause. Thus, there is no stoning (rajm) in the absence of adultery (zinā), and likewise no stoning in the absence of iḥṣān (the state of being married or having been married). But the aspects of negation are what differ. And since the aspects of consideration (jihāt al-naẓar) diverge, multiply in themselves, and differ in their properties, the jurists have conventionally adopted multiple expressions that — by their convention — indicate these purposes. This is the art of jurisprudence (fiqh), and it is what befits it.

The view that deviates from this — namely, positing all attributes as restrictions (quyūd) on the cause, as parts and pillars thereof, on the ground that existence is dependent upon all of them — is derived from the art of theology (kalām), as we have noted. And a genuine disagreement in this matter is not conceivable from the standpoint of meaning; rather, it reduces to mere nomenclature, or to the attribution known by custom, as we have mentioned.

This completes the exposition concerning the prevention of the ruling due to a countervailing impediment (ʿāriḍ mudāfiʿ) that holds the status of a cutter-off (qāṭiʿ), and concerning its prevention due to the loss of a condition and a locus.

Now we turn back to the purpose we were pursuing, namely: the exposition of the occurrence of

؛ فالنظر فيه كثير الجدوى في الفقه، فنقول -وبالله التوفيق -:
المسئلة الواردة نقضا على العلة المظنونة، لا تخلو: أما أن يعلم PageV01P500 # قطعا أنها وردت مورد الاستثناء عن القاعدة لخصوص معنى وحالة؛ أو لم يعلم
كونها واردة على طريق الاستثناء وأستبقاء العلة فيما وراءه.
فإن علم أنها وردت مورد الاستثناء، لم يكن نقضا على العلة جدلا، ولا
ينقطع به ظن المجتهد في مجرى نظره. وبيان ذلك بالمثال: أنا إذا عللنا
-لإيجاب المماثلة بالكيل في الربويات -بعلة الطعم، فأورد علينا مسئلة
العرايا نقضا -لم ينقطع الظن عن العلة [به]: لأنه علم أنه ورد مورد
الاستثناء عن جملة القاعدة، بخصوص حالة؛ والاستثناء صريح في استبقاء
المستثنى [منه]: فإنه لم يرد مورد النسخ لقاعدة الربا، بل ورد مورد اقتطاع
طرف لنوع حاجة. والدليل على كونه استثناء: الإجماع، فإنه وارد على المعلل
بالكيل والقوت والمالية، فكيف يستقيم -في الجدل من هؤلاء -النقض به، وعلتهم
-أيضا -منقوضة به؟ وكيف ينقطع ظن المجتهد عن الطعم، وعلى أي وجه تقلب فهو
مضطر إلى أن يفهم أن الحكم في العرايا لم يرد لدفع قاعدة الربا، بل ورد PageV01P501 # [مقررا لها] بما جرى فيه: من التقييد بخمسة أوسق وغيره. ولكنه اقتطعت
صورته لحاجة مخصوصة؟ وهذا يلحق النظر فيه بالعلة  القطعية، وهو: أن ورود
الاستثناء على العلة يعطف قيدا على العلة. وهل يخرج مطلقها عن أن يسمى علة
أو يضاف الحكم إليه؟ وقد ذكرنا بيانه.
وحد ما يعلم كونه واردا مورد الاستثناء: أن يضطر إليه كل فريق على أي وجه
ردد النظر؛ لا يختص ذلك بمذهب دون مذهب.
فإذا علم المجتهد أنه على أي وجه تقلب في نظره، وعلى أي علة اعتمد: اضطر
إليه -كان ذلك إجماعا في وروده مورد الاستثناء، فلا ينقطع نظره.
وإن كان مجادلا، فلا يلزمه النقض، لأنه منقلب على الخصم في علته ومذهبه
-أيضا -. وهل يجب الاحتراز عنه بصورة لفظ، وتقييد بقيد عبارة؟ اختلف فيه
الجدليون. والأصح -عندنا -: أن تكليف ذلك قبيح في الاصطلاح، كما تقدم.
ومن أمثلة ذك: تمسكنا -في إيجاب تعيين النية في الصوم -بكونه عبادة
مفروضة، فيفتقر إلى التعيين. فقيل [لنا]: يبطل [هذا] PageV01P502 # بالحج، فإنه لا يفتقر إلى التعيين. فأقول: أما المجتهد فلا ينقطع ظنه
الحاصل بمخالفة الحج له؛ فإنه كيف ما تردد، فالحج على خلاف قياس العبادات
في النية؛ فإنه لو أهل بإهلال كإهلال زيد -وهو لا يدري -: انعقد. وتطرق
إليه أمور لا تتطرق إلى سائر العبادات. فعلم أن الشرع قطعه عن قياس غيره،
واستثناء عنه؛ لا أنه رفع به قياس [70 - أ] العبادات. إذ لابد من إتباع نوع
من النظر في افتقار العبادات إلى النية، فكيفما ورد فالحج على مخالفته.
هذا نظر المجتهد. وربما يسنح في هذا المقام أن المعنى المناسب -لو ظهر
-متروك، ووجب العدول إلى التشبيه. وهو: أن الصوم إلى الصلاة أقرب منه [إلى] الحج.
وعلى الجملة: انعطف من الحج قيد وإضافة على العلة المطلقة؛ وذلك القيد لا
يناسب، وإنما هو تمييز بعلامة فاصلة لمحل جريان الحكم -عن محل انقطاعه؛
وهو: الشبه الذي قدمناه. فأما أن يستعمل الشبه والعلامة كاستعمال المخيل
وتخصيصه، وأما أن يعتبر العلامة ويضيف الحكم إلى نفس العلة. ولذلك اضطر
النكرون للتعليل بأوصاف لا تناسب، إلى جواز الاحتراز -في مثل هذه المواضع
-بوصف PageV01P503 # لا يناسب؛ فإنه  مضموم [إلى المناسب] غير مستقل بنفسه. وبه يتبين أن القول
بالعلامات الفاصلة التي لا تناسب -وهو الذي يسمى: الشبه مرة، والطرد أخرى
-حق لا محيص عنه. إذ لو سبر السابر جميع المناسبات المخيلة، لم يصادف واحدا
منها يطرد من غير احتياج إلى تقييد، وتخصيص، وإضافة إلى جنس دون جنس. وتلك
الإضافات: [إضافات] قيود بعلامات لا تناسب؛ كتخصيص معنى مناسب بالبيع،
وقطعه عن النكاح. وتخصيص مناسب بالقصاص، وقطعه عن السرقة؛ مع أن صرف
المناسبة ومحضها ينسب إلى الكل على وتيرة [واحدة]. ولكن يقال: علم أن الشرع
راعى هذا المعنى في موضع دون موضع؛ والتقييد ببعض المواضع على خلاف
المناسبة؛ فالمناسبة منقوضة، ويتعين الرجوع إلى العلامات المعرفة لمجارى
الأحكام ومقاطعها؛ وهو: القول بالوصف الذي لا يناسب في تعريف محل الحكم به،
سمي ذلك شبها أو طردا.
وإذا نبهنا على هذه الدقيقة، فنعود إلى الغرض ونقول: كما لا ينقطع ظن
المجتهد بورود الحج نقضا -: لعلمه بأن الحج يخالف كل قياس PageV01P504 # ذكر، ونزول الحج منزلة العرايا، وكونه نقضا لكل علة ذكرت في الربا
-فليعلم أن المجادل أيضا يدفع النقض بهذا الطريق، ويقول: معول الخصم على
عدم التعيين [في الحج] والحج -أيضا -لا يتعين وقته. وقياسه الافتقار إلى
التعيين. فهو نقض على كل فريق؛ فليخرج من اللبس وليعلم أن حكم الشرع فيه
وارد في معرض قطعه، واستثنائه بخصوص اسمه وصفاته عن غيره. فالنظر في الباقي
-على ما يقتضيه التعليل -مستمر، والحج لا يورد نقضا على شيء منه. فإن
المعلل لا يفارق خصمه في أصل التعليل؛ وإنما يفارقه في عين العلة. والحج
نقض على كل علة عينت، فليس يختص الخصم بالتزامه، وهو على خلاف الكل
بالإجماع. فكأنا عرفنا بالإجماع أن وروده مورد الخصوص والاستثناء، لا مورد
النقض والدفع للقاعدة الجارية. فهذا وما يضاهيه لا يرد نقضا.
ثم للجدليين خلاف: في أن الاحتراز عنه بلفظ، هل يجب؟ كقولنا: صوم، مثلا.
وقد نبهنا عليه، والأمر فيه قريب.
PageV01P505
فإذن الحد في هذا الجنس: أن يعلم بالإجماع وروده على مخالفة  كل قياس، أو
يعلم بإجماع الخصمين وروده على الفريقين. وإذا أحاط الإنسان بهد الحد، علم
أن قول أصحابنا: حق مقصود، فيورث -قياسا لخيار الشرط على خيار [الرد]
بالعيب -منقوض بالأجل. ولا يغنيهم قولهم: أن الأجل خارج عن القياس. لأن
الخصم لا يعترف به، بل يزعم أنه يسويه على قياس نفسه.
وكذلك إذا قلنا: الكتابة الفاسدة خارجة عن القياس، فلا تلزم نقضا في
البيع الفاسد -لم يسمع ذلك؛ لأنها غير خارجة عن قياس مذهب الخصم، على ما
يعتقد في انعقاد الفاسد.
وإن صوم التطوع: إذا ورد نقضا [على] غلتنا في تبييت النية، لم يسمع
قولنا: أنه خارج عن القياس؛ لأن الخصم يزعم أنه غير خارج عن قياسه.
وكذلك: إذا عللنا للمساواة في القصاص في مسئلة [قتل] الحر بالعبد،
والمسلم بالذمي؛ فأورد قتل الجماعة بالواحد نقضا -لم يسمع قولنا: أنه خارج
عن القياس؛ لأن الخصم يزعم أنه جار على قياسه: في أن المساواة غير مرعية،
وأن كل واحد قاتل على الكمال [والتمام] PageV01P506 # إلى نظائر لذلك: اشتهر في المجادلات؛ ولا وجه لشيء من ذلك.
فإن قيل: فالخصم قد يقول: إن استغناء الحج عن التعيين ليس خارجا عن
قياسي، وإنما القرينة عندي تعين، كما أن القصد يعين. فقد حصل التعيين
بالقرينة.
قلنا: إن استقام له ذلك، فتلك المسئلة لا تصلح للتمثيل. [فيرد التمثيل]
إلى مسئلة العرايا: فإنها ترد بالاتفاق على كل فريق؛ ولا يجرى تعليل معلل
فيه بحال.
وإذا ضبطنا قاعدة برابطة وقيدناه بمثال، فإن سنح للناظر في عين ذلك
المثال شيء، فليطلب مثالا أمثل وأقرب منه؛ ولا ينعطف على القاعدة المعلومة
بالإبطال، لما يتطرق إلى الأمثلة من الاختلال. وإنما المقصود أن ورود
المسئلة على الكافة -إذا لم يكن معلوما -لم يسمع مجرد الدعوى بالخروج عن
القياس.
وهذا كله بيان ما علم [أن] وروده مورد الاستثناء [مع أن العلة مظنونة،
فأما إذا لم يعلم وروده مورد الاستثناء] كالتطوع في مسئلة PageV01P507 # تبييت النية -فالاحتراز عنه في الجدل واجب لا شك فيه: إذ لا تبقى إلا
الدعوى المجردة في خروجه عن القاعدة.
أما المجتهد، فهل ينقطع ظنه عن العلة التي ظنها؟ وهل يجوز أن يبقى الظن
مع ورود النقض؟ فقد ردد القاضي -رضي الله عنه -كلامه [في هذا]، وردد رأيه
في أن القول ببطلان العلة بمثل هذا [النقض] معلوم، أم مظنون؟
والتفصيل [70 - ب] الحاوى للغرض فيه -عندي -أن يقال: إن انقدح الاعتذار
عن مسئلة النقض بفقه على مذاق التعليل، [وهو المناسبة: إن كان التعليل
مناسبا؛ أو الشبه: إن كان التعليل] شبها -فلا شك في انقطاع الظن: إذ تبين
به أن ما سنح بعض العلة، وينعطف عليه قيد مناسب. فالعلة مجموع الأمرين.
فإذا قلنا: طهارة فافتقرت إلى النية"، وانتقض بإزالة النجاسة -وجب
التقييد بأنها طهارة حكمية. وظهر للمجتهد والمجادل أن علامة الحكم كلا
الوصفين، لا أحدهما.
وكذلك: إذا كانت العلة مخيلة، وانقدح عذر مخيل ينضاف إلى الأول ويصير
جزءا منه -فلا شك في أن العلة صارت منقوضة، وانعطف عليها قيد.
PageV01P508
أما إذا كانت العلة مخيلة، وكان لا ينقدح في مسئلة النقض عذر وجه من
الوجوه -ولنقدر مثاله: التطوع في مسئلة التبييت؛ إذ المعنى المخيل: أن
العبادة تفتقر إلى النية، والنية لا تنعطف على ما مضى، وأول العبادة لا
يستغنى عن النية؛ فهذا كلام مناسب مخيل، وهو منقوض بالتطوع، ولنقدر أنه ليس
ينقدح في التطوع عذر مخيل على مذاق العلة، وهو كذلك -فالظن الذي ذكرناه هل
ينقطع بورود التطوع.؟ هذا محل [النظر: إذ يحتمل] أن يجعل التطوع معرفا
لفساد العلة، ويحتمل أن يجعل استثناء بخصوص صفة مع بقاء العلة التي ذكرناها
معتبرة. وقد تردد الأصوليون في هذا؛ وأنا أفصل القول في جنسه، فأقول:
إن كان المناسب -الذي ذكره المعلل -على رتبة لا يستقل بنفسه مرسلا،
ويفتقر إلى أصل يشهد له -كما قدمنا فيه التفصيل -: انقطع الظن بالنقض: لأنه
لا طريق [إلى معرفة] كونه علة إلا شهادة الحكم له بوروده على وفقه. كما
ذكرنا طريق التعليل بالمناسبات.
وإذا كان يعتقد صحته بورود الشرع على وفقه؛ فمسئلة النقض على  خلافه -تشهد
بأنه ليس ملحوظا. فمن أعطى فقيرا ولم يذكر سببه، ظننا أنه أعطاه: لكونه
فقيرا. إذ الفقر مناسب يصلح أن PageV01P509 # يكون باعثا. فإذا حرم فقيرا مثله في الفقر: علم أن الفقر لم يكن باعثا،
وانقطع الظن؛ أو علم أن الفقر مع وصف آخر كان باعثا، وقد عدم ذلك الوصف في
الفقير الآخر، ولسنا نطلع عليه، فهذا الجنس يقطع بانقطاع الظن فيه.
فأما إذا كانت المناسبة على رتبة لا تفتقر إلى شهادة الأصل، وهو: المعنى
الملائم والمؤثر -كما ضربنا أمثلته في الاستدلال المرسل -فإذا ورد نقص
عليه، واحتمل أن يكون قد سلك به مسلك الاستثناء -فلست أجل بقاء الظن وحمل
النقض على الخصوص والاستثناء بخصوص حالة.
ولست أعني بالمناسب المستغني عن الأصل: الوصف الذي دل الإجماع أو النص
على كونه مؤثرا في عين الحكم؛ فإن ذلك يلتحق بالعلة المعلومة، وهو الذي زعم
أبو زيد -رضي الله عنه -أنه مشروط في العلل، ولم يقبل عليه النقض. وذلك سبق
مثاله في المصراة، وضرب الدية على العاقلة.
ولكن: ربما تعرف العلة بالظن لا بالعلم اليقيني، ويكون استدلالا مرسلا
بمعنى يلائم تصرفات الشرع، وورود النقض عليه لا يقطع الظن. وأقرب مثال له.
مسئلة [تبييت النية]؛ فإن قولنا: العبادات مفتقرة إلى النية"، كلام معلوم.
وقولنا: أن كل اليوم يجب صومه"، [كلام] PageV01P510 # معلوم. وقولنا: أن [صوم بعض] اليوم بعض العبادة وقد خلا عن النية"،
معلوم. وقولنا: أن النية عزم وقصد لا ينعطف على الماضي"، معلوم في العقل؛
وعدم انعطافه حكما مظنون، مستنده: عدم انعطافه عقلا وتحقيقا.
فهذا كلام لا يفتقر إلى الاستشهاد بالقضاء؛ ولكنه منقوض بالتطوع. ولا
[يخطرن الناظر بالبال] منع بعض المتقدمين أن العبادة من PageV01P511 # التطوع: بعض اليوم؛ فذلك من المنكرات في الشرع. فإذا نظر المجتهد في
التطوع، احتمل عنده احتمال الشرع انعطاف النية على السابق حكما؛ وإن لم
ينعطف تحقيقا. واحتمل أن يقال: استثنى التطوع عن هذه القضية: رخصة، وترغيبا
في تكثير النوافل، وتساهلا فيها. فلقد تساهل الشرع في النوافل في أمور فارق
فيها  الفرائض. ولو كان كذلك: لبقيت العلة التي ظهرت أولا باقية في الظن؛
ولو كان بخلافه: لا ينقض. وليس يبعد أن يترجح للمجتهد ظن الاستثناء على ظن
الإبطال؛ فيعتمده. فهذا في محل الاجتهاد، ويختلف بآحاد المسائل، وبقوة
المناسبات وبظهور وجه خيال الاستثناء.
وحظ الأصول أن كلا الأمرين مجوز في الإمكان، والنظر في تعيين آحاد
المسائل إلى المجتهد. ثم إذا استقر الظن على العلة السابقة للمجتهد، فطريق
المجادل: أما الاحتراز ظاهرا، وأما الإبداء للمقصود إجراء على ما يجرى به
رسم الاصطلاح، وهو: أن يبين أن ظن الاستثناء -مع ظن إبقاء المعنى معتبرا
-أغلب من ظن الانعطاف على المعنى بالإبطال. وعند هذا تكاد تظهر الحاجة إلى
الاستشهاد بالقضاء: لنتبين به أن هذا المعنى لم PageV01P512 # يعطله الشرع مطلقا، بل أبقاه مستعملا في الفرض. والأداء: بأن يكون محل
استعماله، كما كان القضاء محل استعماله -أولى من أن يكون محل تعطيله. كما
في التطوع.
وبالاحتياج إلى هذا الاستشهاد، يتبين أن التعلق بالعلامة الشبهية أولى من
التعلق بالمناسبة التي لا تطرد؛ فإن الحكم إن كان يتبع المناسبة المحضة:
فقد صارت منقوضة. وإن كان يتبع العلامة الحاصرة القاطعة لمجرى الحكم عن
موقعه -وهو: علامة الفرضية -: فليتعلق به [71 - أ] بطريق الشبه، كما سبق.
وكل متعلق بمناسبة فهو مضطر إلى تقييد مناسبته بقيود، وتخصيصها بمواضع. مع
أن المناسبة لا تختص بتلك القيود.
ولأجله قال قائلون -وبه تشبث أبو زيد -رضي الله عنه -: أن المناسبة لا
وجه للتعلق بها، ولكن الأوصاف -التي عقل من الشرع ضبط الأحكام بها، وعرفت
فواصل بين النفي والإثبات بموارد الشرع
PageV01P513
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ث ن ي (th-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Doubling, folding back; secondary occurrence; repetition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Istithnāʾ (exception) as a legal-technical act of setting apart a case from a general rule (mustathnā minhu) while preserving the rule's validity for the remainder.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense — drawing out one item from a set; metaphorical extension — the juristic exception that does not abrogate (naskh) but delimits (takhṣīṣ).
- Root: ق ط ع (q-ṭ-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cutting off, severing; decisive separation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Uṣūl al-Fiqh, the "cutting off" of a cause's operation (inqiṭāʿ al-ẓann) — the decisive termination of the jurist's probable judgment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical severance; metaphorical — the definitive demarcation (qāṭiʿah) between the domain where a rule runs and where it ceases.
- Root: ش ب ه (sh-b-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Resemblance, similarity; ambiguity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Shabah (the "resemblance" type of cause) — a non-appropriate (ghayr munāsib) descriptive mark that nonetheless serves as a legal indicator (ʿalāmah) for the scope of a ruling.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — visual similarity; metaphorical — the juristic "mark" (ʿalāmah) that distinguishes cases, as opposed to the self-sufficient appropriate meaning (al-munāsib al-muʾaththir).
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-Ḥukm ʿalā al-ʿIllah maʿa al-Istithnāʾ (Attributing a ruling to a cause while an exception is appended) — The exception functions syntactically as a restrictive qualifier (qayd) that attaches to the cause, not as a negation of the cause's general applicability.
chapters.translation:
I say — and with God is success:

The question posed as a counter-example (naqḍ) against a probable cause (al-ʿillah al-maẓnūnah) admits of only two cases: either it is known with certainty that it came as an exception (istithnāʾ) to the general rule, due to a specific meaning and circumstance; or it is not known that it came by way of exception, with the cause remaining operative beyond it.

If it is known that it came as an exception, then it is not, dialectically, a counter-example against the cause, nor does it cut off the jurist's probable judgment (ẓann) in the course of his reasoning. The clarification of this is by example: when we assign, for the obligation of equivalence (al-mumāthalah) in ribawī transactions by measure (kayl), the cause of taste (ṭaʿm), and the case of ʿarāyā (the sale of fresh dates on the tree for dried dates) is brought against us as a counter-example — the probable judgment is not cut off from the cause by it. For it is known that it came as an exception to the body of the rule, due to a specific circumstance; and the exception is explicit in preserving what is excepted from (al-mustathnā minhu). For it did not come by way of abrogation (naskh) of the rule of ribā, but rather by way of cutting off a segment for a specific need. The proof that it is an exception is the consensus (ijmāʿ): for it applies against one who assigns the cause as measure, or as sustenance (qūt), or as monetary value (māliyyah). How then, in dialectic among these, could the counter-example stand against them, when their own cause is also countered by it? And how could the jurist's probable judgment be cut off from taste, when on whatever face he turns, he is compelled to understand that the ruling in ʿarāyā did not come to repudiate the rule of ribā, but rather came to confirm it, by what occurred therein — the restriction to five wasq and other conditions — yet its form was cut off for a specific need? This attaches its consideration to the certain cause (al-ʿillah al-qaṭʿiyyah), namely: that the occurrence of an exception upon a cause attaches a qualifier (qayd) to the cause. And does its absolute form cease to be called a cause, or is the ruling attributed to it? We have already stated its clarification.

The limit by which it is known that something came as an exception is: that every party is compelled to it, on whatever face the reasoning is turned; it is not peculiar to one school (madhhab) to the exclusion of another.

So when the jurist knows that on whatever face he turns in his reasoning, and on whatever cause he relies, he is compelled to it — that is a consensus (ijmāʿ) on its coming as an exception, and his reasoning is not cut off.

And if he is a disputant (mujādil), the counter-example does not bind him, because it rebounds against the opponent in his own cause and his own school as well. And is it obligatory to guard against it by a verbal form, and to restrict it by a qualifier of expression? The dialecticians have differed on this. The more correct view with us is that imposing that is repugnant (qabīḥ) in convention (iṣṭilāḥ), as has preceded.

Among its examples: our argument, for the obligation of specifying the intention (taʿyīn al-niyyah) in fasting, that it is an obligatory act of worship (ʿibādah mafrūḍah), and thus requires specification. It was said to us: this is invalidated by the Pilgrimage (ḥajj), for it does not require specification. I say: as for the jurist, his probable judgment, obtained by the Pilgrimage's differing from it, is not cut off. For however he deliberates, the Pilgrimage runs contrary to the analogy (qiyās) of acts of worship regarding intention; for if one enters the state of iḥrām with an intention like that of Zayd — while not knowing — it is validly contracted. And matters attach to it that do not attach to other acts of worship. Thus it is known that the Lawgiver cut it off from analogy to others, and made it an exception from it; not that He raised the analogy of acts of worship by it. For one must follow some mode of reasoning in the dependence of acts of worship upon intention; so however it comes, the Pilgrimage runs contrary to it. This is the jurist's reasoning.

And perhaps it occurs at this juncture that the appropriate meaning (al-maʿnā al-munāsib) — were it to appear — is abandoned, and one must turn to resemblance (tashbīh). That is: fasting is closer to prayer than it is to the Pilgrimage.

In sum: from the Pilgrimage there turns back a qualifier and an addition upon the absolute cause; and that qualifier is not appropriate (munāsib), but is rather a distinguishing mark (ʿalāmah fāṣilah) for the locus where the ruling runs — as opposed to the locus where it ceases; and this is the resemblance (shabah) we have mentioned. Either the resemblance and the mark are used like the use of the appropriate cause (al-mukhīl) and its specification, or the mark is considered and the ruling is attributed to the cause itself. For this reason, those who deny causation by non-appropriate attributes were compelled to permit guarding against such cases by a non-appropriate attribute — for it is annexed to the appropriate one, not independent by itself. By this it becomes clear that the doctrine of distinguishing marks that are not appropriate — which is called "resemblance" at times and "ṭard" (coextension) at others — is true, with no escape from it. For were an investigator to survey all the appropriate meanings (al-munāsabāt al-mukhīlah), he would not encounter a single one that runs coextensively without needing restriction, specification, and addition to one genus rather than another. And those additions are additions of qualifiers by non-appropriate marks — like specifying an appropriate meaning to sale (bayʿ) and cutting it off from marriage (nikāḥ); and specifying an appropriate meaning to retaliation (qiṣāṣ) and cutting it off from theft (sariqah) — even though the pure and unmixed appropriateness relates to all on one uniform footing. But it is said: it is known that the Lawgiver observed this meaning in one locus and not another; and the restriction to some loci is contrary to appropriateness; so the appropriateness is countered (manqūḍah), and one must return to the marks that define the courses of rulings and their terminations — namely, the doctrine of the non-appropriate attribute in defining the locus of the ruling by it, whether that be called resemblance or ṭard.

Now that we have drawn attention to this subtlety, we return to the purpose and say: just as the jurist's probable judgment is not cut off by the Pilgrimage's coming as a counter-example — because of his knowledge that the Pilgrimage runs contrary to every analogy mentioned, and that the Pilgrimage holds the station of ʿarāyā, being a counter-example to every cause mentioned in ribā — so too let it be known that the disputant also repels the counter-example by this path, and says: the opponent's reliance is upon the absence of specification in the Pilgrimage, and the Pilgrimage's time is also not specified; and his analogy is the dependence upon specification. So it is a counter-example against every party; let him emerge from confusion and know that the Lawgiver's ruling therein came in the mode of cutting it off and excepting it, by the specificity of its name and attributes, from others. Thus the reasoning concerning the remainder — according to what the causation requires — continues, and the Pilgrimage is not brought as a counter-example against any part of it. For the one who assigns the cause does not part from his opponent in the principle of causation; he only parts from him in the specific cause (ʿayn al-ʿillah). And the Pilgrimage is a counter-example to every specific cause assigned, so the opponent is not uniquely bound by it; and it runs contrary to all, by consensus. It is as if we knew by consensus that its coming was in the mode of specificity and exception, not in the mode of counter-example and repudiation of the running rule. So this and what resembles it do not come as counter-examples.

Then there is a dispute among the dialecticians: whether guarding against it by a word is obligatory — like our saying, for example, "fasting." We have already drawn attention to this, and the matter is near at hand.

So the limit in this genus is: that it be known by consensus that it came contrary to every analogy, or that it be known by the consensus of both opponents that it came against both parties. When one encompasses this limit, he knows that the saying of our companions — that the option of stipulation (khiyār al-sharṭ) is rightly intended, so that analogizing it to the option of defect (khiyār al-ʿayb) is countered by the term (ajal) — is not sufficient. Nor does their saying avail them: that the term is outside the analogy. For the opponent does not concede this; rather, he claims that it is equal to his own analogy.

Likewise, when we say: the invalid contract of kitābah (manumission by written agreement) is outside the analogy, so it does not bind as a counter-example in the invalid sale — this is not heard; for it is not outside the analogy of the opponent's school, according to what he believes regarding the validity of the invalid (contract).

And if voluntary fasting (ṣawm al-taṭawwuʿ) comes as a counter-example against our cause in the overnight intention (tabyīt al-niyyah), our saying that it is outside the analogy is not heard; for the opponent claims that it is not outside his analogy.

Likewise, when we assign as cause for equality in retaliation in the case of killing a free man for a slave, and a Muslim for a dhimmī, and the killing of a group for one is brought as a counter-example — our saying that it is outside the analogy is not heard; for the opponent claims that it runs according to his analogy: that equality is not observed, and that each one is a killer in full and complete measure. And similar cases are well-known in disputations; and none of that has any validity.

If it is said: the opponent may say that the Pilgrimage's independence from specification is not outside my analogy; rather, in my view, the contextual indicator (qarīnah) specifies, just as the intention specifies; so specification is achieved by the contextual indicator.

We say: if that holds for him, then that question is not suitable for exemplification. So the exemplification reverts to the case of ʿarāyā: for it applies by agreement against every party; and no causation of any causer runs in it at all.

Now that we have fixed the rule with a bond and restricted it with an example, if something occurs to the investigator regarding that very example, let him seek a better and closer example; and let him not turn upon the known rule with invalidation, because of the defect that attaches to examples. The purpose is only that the question's applying to all — when it is not known — mere claim of being outside the analogy is not heard.

All this is the clarification of what is known to have come as an exception [while the cause is probable]. As for when it is not known to have come as an exception — like voluntary fasting in the question of overnight intention — then guarding against it in dialectic is obligatory, with no doubt: for nothing remains but the mere claim of its being outside the rule.

As for the jurist: is his probable judgment cut off from the cause he deemed probable? And is it permissible for the probable judgment to remain with the occurrence of the counter-example? The Judge (al-Qāḍī) — may God be pleased with him — vacillated in his statement on this, and vacillated in his opinion as to whether the doctrine of the cause's invalidity by such a counter-example is known (maʿlūm) or probable (maẓnūn).

The detailed account that encompasses the purpose therein — in my view — is to say: if an excuse (iʿtidhār) for the counter-example question becomes evident by a jurisprudence (fiqh) according to the taste of the causation — namely, appropriateness (munāsabah) if the cause is appropriate, or resemblance (shabah) if the cause is a resemblance — then there is no doubt about the cutting off of the probable judgment: for by it, it becomes clear that what occurred was part of the cause, and a suitable qualifier turns back upon it. So the cause is the sum of both matters.

Thus when we say: "a purification (ṭahārah) that requires intention," and it is countered by the removal of impurity (izālat al-najāsah) — it becomes obligatory to qualify it as a "ruling purification" (ṭahārah ḥukmiyyah). And it becomes clear to the jurist and the disputant that the mark of the ruling is both attributes, not one of them.

Likewise, if the cause is appropriate (mukhīlah), and an appropriate excuse becomes evident that is annexed to the first and becomes a part of it — then there is no doubt that the cause has become countered, and a qualifier has turned back upon it.

As for when the cause is appropriate, and no excuse becomes evident in the counter-example question by any of the ways — let us suppose its example: voluntary fasting in the question of overnight intention. For the appropriate meaning is: that the act of worship requires intention, and intention does not turn back upon what has passed, and the beginning of the act of worship cannot dispense with intention. This is appropriate, suitable speech, and it is countered by voluntary fasting. Let us suppose that no appropriate excuse becomes evident in voluntary fasting according to the taste of the cause — and such is the case — then is the probable judgment we mentioned cut off by the occurrence of voluntary fasting? This is the locus of inquiry: for it is possible to make voluntary fasting a marker of the cause's corruption, and it is possible to make it an exception by a specific attribute, with the cause we mentioned remaining operative. The Uṣūliyyūn have vacillated on this; and I will give a detailed statement on its genus, saying:

If the appropriate meaning — which the causer mentioned — is at a rank where it is not independent by itself, sent unrestrictedly (mursal), and requires a root (aṣl) to testify for it — as we have detailed before — then the probable judgment is cut off by the counter-example: for there is no path to knowing it is a cause except the testimony of the ruling for it, by its coming in accordance with it, as we mentioned in the path of causation by appropriate meanings.

And if it is believed sound by the Law's coming in accordance with it, then the counter-example question running contrary to it testifies that it is not observed. Thus if someone gives to a poor man without mentioning his reason, we suppose he gave him because he is poor — for poverty is appropriate, fit to be a motive. Then if he withholds from another poor man equal in poverty, we know that poverty was not the motive, and the probable judgment is cut off; or we know that poverty with another attribute was the motive, and that attribute was absent in the other poor man, though we do not discover it. This genus is decisive in the cutting off of the probable judgment.

As for when the appropriateness is at a rank that does not require the testimony of the root — namely, the suitable and effective meaning (al-maʿnā al-mulāʾim wa al-muʾaththir) — as we have given its examples in the unrestricted inference (al-istidlāl al-mursal) — then if a counter-example comes upon it, and it is possible that it has been treated by way of exception — then I do not judge the cutting off of the probable judgment, nor the carrying of the counter-example upon specificity and exception by a specific circumstance.

By the appropriate meaning independent of the root, I do not mean the attribute that consensus or the text has indicated to be effective in the very ruling; for that attaches to the known cause, and it is what Abū Zayd — may God be pleased with him — claimed to be a condition in causes, and he did not accept counter-examples against it. Its example has preceded in the case of the muṣarrāh (the milk-retained animal) and the imposition of the blood-wit (diyah) upon the ʿāqilah (the paternal relatives).

But rather: the cause is sometimes known by probable judgment, not by certain knowledge, and it is an unrestricted inference by a meaning that suits the Lawgiver's acts; and the occurrence of a counter-example upon it does not cut off the probable judgment. The closest example to it is the question of overnight intention. For our saying "acts of worship require intention" is known speech. And our saying "the entire day must be fasted" is known speech. And our saying "part of the day is part of the act of worship, and it has been devoid of intention" is known. And our saying "intention is resolve and purpose that does not turn back upon the past" is known in the intellect; and its not turning back as a ruling is probable, whose basis is its not turning back intellectually and in reality.

So this speech does not require seeking testimony from the make-up (qaḍāʾ); but it is countered by voluntary fasting. And let not the investigator entertain the denial of some of the predecessors that the act of worship in voluntary fasting is part of the day; for that is among the repugnant things in the Law. So when the jurist considers voluntary fasting, it is possible in his view — by the Law's possibility — that intention turns back upon the prior part as a ruling, even if it does not turn back in reality. And it is possible to say: the Lawgiver excepted voluntary fasting from this proposition — as a concession (rukḥṣah), an encouragement to multiply supererogatory acts, and an indulgence in them. For the Lawgiver has indulged in supererogatory acts in matters wherein they differ from the obligatory. And were it so, the cause that first appeared would remain operative in the probable judgment; and were it otherwise, it would not be countered. Nor is it far that the probable judgment of exception should outweigh, for the jurist, the probable judgment of invalidation; so he relies upon it. This, then, is in the locus of ijtihād, and it varies with individual questions, with the strength of the appropriate meanings, and with the evidentness of the aspect of the exception's imagination.

The share of Uṣūl is that both matters are permissible in possibility, and the consideration of determining individual questions belongs to the jurist. Then, when the probable judgment settles upon the prior cause for the jurist, the disputant's path is either to guard against it outwardly, or to set forth the intended course according to what the convention's practice runs upon — namely, that he show that the probable judgment of exception — with the probable judgment of keeping the meaning operative — is more preponderant than the probable judgment of turning upon the meaning by invalidation. And at this point the need for seeking testimony from the make-up (qaḍāʾ) nearly appears: to show by it that this meaning was not nullified by the Lawgiver absolutely, but rather He kept it operative in the obligatory. And the performance (adāʾ) — in that it is the locus of its operation, just as the make-up was the locus of its operation — is more fitting than being the locus of its nullification, as in voluntary fasting.

And by the need for this testimony, it becomes clear that attachment to the resemblance-mark (al-ʿalāmah al-shabahiyyah) is more fitting than attachment to the appropriateness that does not run coextensively. For if the ruling follows pure appropriateness, then it has become countered. And if it follows the encompassing mark that cuts off the course of the ruling from its locus — namely, the mark of obligatoriness (al-farḍiyyah) — then let one attach to it by way of resemblance, as has preceded.

And everyone who attaches to an appropriateness is compelled to restrict his appropriateness with qualifiers, and to specify it to loci — even though the appropriateness is not peculiar to those qualifiers.

And for this reason, some said — and Abū Zayd — may God be pleased with him — clung to this: that appropriateness has no aspect for attachment; but rather the attributes by which the Lawgiver's regulation of rulings is understood, and by which the separators between negation and affirmation are known through the Law's sources —

chapters.title_en: Section 97 — On the Naming of Cause (ʿIllah) and the Attachment of a Ruling to Two Causes
